grammar.title: Modal Verb CAN for Ability
grammar.explanation: In English, we use 'can' to express ability or possibility. Unlike Spanish where 'poder' conjugates (puedo, puedes, puede), 'can' NEVER changes form regardless of the subject. It is always followed by the base form of the verb (infinitive without 'to'). For negatives, we use 'cannot' or the contraction 'can't'.
grammar.rule: After 'can' or 'can't', always use the verb in its base form without 'to'.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students often say 'I can to sing' because in Spanish we use the infinitive 'Yo puedo cantar'. In English, we NEVER use 'to' after 'can'.

examples.es: Puedo nadar muy rápido.

examples.es: Ella todavía no puede manejar un carro.

examples.es: ¿Puedes hablar francés?

commonErrors.why: Never use 'to' after 'can'. Use the base form of the verb.
'Can' never takes an 's' in third person. It stays the same for all subjects.

grammar.title: Negative Form with CAN'T
grammar.explanation: To make negative sentences with 'can', we use 'cannot' (one word, formal) or 'can't' (contraction, common in speaking). The structure is the same as positive: subject + can't + base verb. In Spanish, you say 'no puedo cantar', placing 'no' before the verb. In English, 'can't' is one unit that replaces both 'no' and changes 'can'.
grammar.rule: Use 'can't' or 'cannot' before the base verb to express inability.
grammar.spanishTrap: Students sometimes say 'I no can dance' copying the Spanish 'yo no puedo bailar'. In English, we never separate 'not' from 'can' - they form 'can't'.

grammar.title: Yes/No Questions with CAN
grammar.explanation: To form questions with 'can', we invert the order: 'Can' comes before the subject. Unlike Spanish where you can keep the same word order and just change intonation ('¿Tú puedes nadar?'), English requires inversion for questions. The verb after the subject remains in base form.
grammar.rule: In questions, 'can' comes before the subject, followed by the base verb.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students may say 'You can swim?' keeping Spanish word order. In English, questions with 'can' must start with 'Can' for yes/no questions.

grammar.title: Using CAN for abilities and possibilities
grammar.explanation: In English, 'can' is a modal verb that expresses ability (what someone is able to do) and possibility. Unlike Spanish where 'poder' changes form (puedo, puedes, puede), 'can' NEVER changes form regardless of the subject. The negative form is 'can't' or 'cannot'.
grammar.rule: After 'can', always use the base form of the verb without 'to'.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers often add 'to' after can (wrong: 'I can to swim') because in Spanish you say 'puedo nadar' but translate it literally as 'I can to swim'. Also, students try to conjugate the main verb (wrong: 'She can speaks') because Spanish changes the main verb form.

examples.en: I can play the guitar.
examples.es: Puedo tocar la guitarra.

examples.en: She can speak French.
examples.es: Ella puede hablar francés.

examples.en: They can't go swimming today.
examples.es: Ellos no pueden ir a nadar hoy.

commonErrors.why: Don't use 'to' after 'can'. Use the base form of the verb.
After 'can', use the base form without -s, even with he/she/it.

grammar.title: Question formation with CAN
grammar.explanation: To form questions with 'can', we invert the subject and 'can' (not like Spanish where you just change intonation or add question marks). Information questions start with a question word (what, when, who, where, why), followed by 'can', then the subject, then the base verb. Unlike Spanish, word order changes in English questions.
grammar.structure: Question word + can + subject + base verb?
grammar.rule: For yes/no questions: Can + subject + base verb? For information questions: Question word + can + subject + base verb?
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers often forget to invert subject and 'can' because in Spanish you can just say '¿Tú puedes hablar inglés?' without changing word order. In English, you MUST say 'Can you speak English?' not 'You can speak English?'

examples.en: Can you help me?
examples.es: ¿Puedes ayudarme?

examples.en: What can we make for dinner?
examples.es: ¿Qué podemos hacer para la cena?

examples.en: When can she go to the bank?
examples.es: ¿Cuándo puede ella ir al banco?

commonErrors.why: In yes/no questions, put 'can' before the subject.
In information questions, the order is: question word + can + subject + verb.

drillSentences.hint: Question word + can + subject + base verb

grammar.title: Word order when WHO is the subject
grammar.explanation: When 'who' asks about the subject of the sentence (the person doing the action), we don't invert the word order. We use 'who + can + verb' just like a statement. This is different from other question words. Compare: 'What can you do?' (what = object) vs 'Who can speak French?' (who = subject).
grammar.rule: When 'who' is the subject, don't invert: Who can + verb (not: Who can + subject + verb).
grammar.spanishTrap: This is similar to Spanish '¿Quién puede hablar?' but students sometimes add an extra subject like 'Who can he speak?' when they mean 'Who can speak?' because they're used to including the subject in other question types.

commonErrors.correct: Who can call you? OR Who can you call?
commonErrors.why: These mean different things. First = who is the subject (who will call). Second = who is the object (you will call whom).
After 'can', always use base form, never add -s.

grammar.title: Making requests and asking for help with CAN
grammar.explanation: We use 'Can you...?' to make polite requests and ask someone to do something for us. This is a very common and useful structure in daily English. In Colombian Spanish, you might say '¿Puedes...?' or '¿Me puedes...?' and English works similarly. We often add 'please' to be more polite.
grammar.structure: Can you + base verb (+ object) + please?
grammar.rule: Can you + base verb makes a polite request for someone to do something.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers sometimes say 'You can help me?' instead of 'Can you help me?' because they forget to invert the subject and modal in questions. Also, adding 'to me' is common in Spanish ('¿Me puedes ayudar?') but in English we usually say 'Can you help me?' not 'Can you to me help?'

examples.en: Can you help me with this problem?
examples.es: ¿Puedes ayudarme con este problema?

examples.en: Can you call the doctor, please?
examples.es: ¿Puedes llamar al doctor, por favor?

examples.en: Can you open the window?
examples.es: ¿Puedes abrir la ventana?

commonErrors.why: Invert 'can' and subject in questions, and don't use 'to' after 'can'.

commonErrors.wrong: Can you to close the door?
commonErrors.why: Never use 'to' after 'can'. Use the base form of the verb.

grammar.title: Should and Shouldn't for Advice
grammar.explanation: We use 'should' and 'shouldn't' to give advice or recommendations. Unlike Spanish where you might use 'debes' (obligation) or 'deberías' (advice), English 'should' is always for advice, not strong obligation. After 'should' or 'shouldn't', we ALWAYS use the base form of the verb (infinitive without 'to').
grammar.rule: Use 'should' for positive advice and 'shouldn't' for negative advice, always followed by the base form of the verb.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian Spanish speakers often add 'to' after 'should' (should to go) or conjugate the verb (should goes). Remember: should + BASE FORM only.

examples.en: You should stay at home today.
examples.es: Deberías quedarte en casa hoy.

examples.en: She should see a doctor.
examples.es: Ella debería ver a un médico.

examples.en: They shouldn't go to work.
examples.es: Ellos no deberían ir al trabajo.

commonErrors.why: 'Should' is already a modal verb, so we don't use 'to' after it.
After 'should', use the base form of the verb, not the conjugated form.

grammar.title: Have + Ailment (Health Problems)
grammar.explanation: In English, we use 'have' + article + ailment to describe health problems. Unlike Spanish where you say 'me duele la cabeza' (literally 'the head hurts me'), English uses the structure 'I have a headache'. Most ailments use the article 'a', but some use no article (like 'have pain').
grammar.rule: Use 'have' or 'has' with 'a' or 'an' before most ailments to describe health problems.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish uses 'tener' with body parts differently. Don't translate literally 'me duele' as 'hurts me'. Instead, use the pattern 'I have a + ailment'.

examples.en: I have a headache.
examples.es: Tengo dolor de cabeza.

examples.en: She has a cold.
examples.es: Ella tiene un resfriado.

examples.en: He has a fever.
examples.es: Él tiene fiebre.

commonErrors.why: Most ailments need the article 'a' before them.
In English, we say 'I have a headache', not 'my head hurts me'.

grammar.title: Frequency Adverbs (sometimes, never, right now)
grammar.explanation: Frequency adverbs tell us HOW OFTEN something happens. In English, these adverbs usually go BEFORE the main verb but AFTER the verb 'to be'. This is different from Spanish where position is more flexible. 'Right now' is an exception and goes at the beginning or end of a sentence.
grammar.structure: Subject + frequency adverb + main verb OR Subject + be + frequency adverb
grammar.rule: Place frequency adverbs (sometimes, never, always) before the main verb but after 'be'.
grammar.spanishTrap: In Spanish, you can say 'Yo tengo a veces' or 'A veces yo tengo', but in English, 'sometimes' must go before the main verb: 'I sometimes have'.

examples.en: I sometimes have a headache at work.
examples.es: A veces tengo dolor de cabeza en el trabajo.

examples.en: I never have a cold.
examples.es: Nunca tengo un resfriado.

examples.en: Right now I have a backache.
examples.es: Ahora mismo tengo dolor de espalda.

commonErrors.why: The frequency adverb goes before the main verb, not after it.
Don't use double negatives in English like in Spanish.

grammar.title: Modal Verb SHOULD for Advice
grammar.explanation: In English, we use 'should' to give advice or recommendations. Unlike Spanish where 'deberías' changes for each person (deberías, debería, deberían), 'should' stays the same for all subjects. After 'should', we always use the base form of the verb (without 'to'). The negative is 'shouldn't' (should not).
grammar.rule: Use 'should' + base verb to give advice; it never changes form regardless of the subject.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students often add 'to' after 'should' (wrong: 'You should to rest') because in Spanish we say 'deberías descansar'. In English, no 'to' is needed after modal verbs.

examples.en: You should rest when you're sick.
examples.es: Deberías descansar cuando estás enfermo.

examples.en: She shouldn't go to school if she has a fever.
examples.es: Ella no debería ir a la escuela si tiene fiebre.

commonErrors.why: Never use 'to' after modal verbs like should, can, must, will.
After 'should', always use the base form of the verb (go, not goes).

grammar.title: Verb LOOK + Adjective (Appearance)
grammar.explanation: In English, we use 'look' + adjective to describe someone's appearance or how they seem. This is similar to Spanish 'verse' or 'parecer'. Unlike Spanish where we might say 'te ves bueno' or 'te ves bien', in English we must say 'you look good' (adjective). Common expressions: look tired, look sick, look happy, look sad.
grammar.rule: Use 'look' + adjective to describe how someone appears or seems.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students might say 'You look well' when they mean 'You look good'. 'Well' is for health or doing something skillfully, but 'good' describes appearance. Also, don't forget 'looks' with he/she/it.

examples.en: You don't look good. Are you sick?
examples.es: No te ves bien. ¿Estás enfermo?

examples.en: She looks tired after the long trip.

commonErrors.why: With he/she/it, add 's' to the verb: looks, not look.

commonErrors.why: This is actually correct—use 'look good' for appearance and 'feel well' for health.

grammar.title: Social Language: Showing Concern
grammar.explanation: When someone is sick or upset, English has specific phrases to show you care. 'What's wrong?' asks about the problem. 'Feel better!' is what you say to wish someone recovery (like '¡Mejórate!' in Spanish). These are fixed expressions—you can't translate them word-by-word. Also use 'I hope you feel better soon' or 'Take care of yourself'.
grammar.structure: What's wrong? / Feel better! / I hope you...
grammar.rule: Use fixed social expressions to show concern; they don't translate word-by-word from Spanish.
grammar.spanishTrap: Don't say 'Get better!' thinking it's like '¡Mejórate!' The correct expression is 'Feel better!' Also, 'What's wrong?' is the natural way to ask, not 'What do you have?' (literal translation of '¿Qué tienes?').

examples.es: ¿Qué te pasa? Te ves molesto.

examples.en: I'm sick today. - Oh no! Feel better soon!

commonErrors.wrong: What you have? You don't look good.
commonErrors.correct: What's wrong? You don't look good.
commonErrors.why: 'What's wrong?' is the natural way to ask about a problem, not 'What do you have?'

grammar.title: Using adjectives to describe feelings with 'be'
grammar.explanation: In English, we use the verb 'to be' (am/is/are) + adjective to describe how someone feels. Unlike Spanish where you use 'estar' for temporary states, English uses the same verb 'be' for both permanent and temporary states. The structure is: subject + be + feeling adjective.
grammar.rule: Use 'be' + adjective (not 'have' + noun like in Spanish) to describe feelings.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian Spanish speakers often say 'I have angry' (Tengo rabia) instead of 'I am angry'. In English, feelings use 'be' + adjective, not 'have' + noun.

grammar.title: Modal verbs: should/shouldn't for advice
grammar.explanation: We use 'should' and 'shouldn't' to give advice or recommendations. After 'should/shouldn't', we always use the base form of the verb (infinitive without 'to'). Unlike Spanish 'debería', which changes form, 'should' stays the same for all subjects (I/you/he/she/we/they should).
grammar.rule: After should/shouldn't, always use the base form of the verb (no 'to', no -ing, no conjugation).
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian speakers often add 'to' after 'should' (like 'debería + infinitivo'), saying 'You should to rest' instead of 'You should rest'. English doesn't use 'to' after modal verbs.

examples.en: She should rest if she's sick.

commonErrors.why: Don't use 'to' after modal verbs like 'should'.
Use base form (rest), not third person form (rests) after 'should'.

grammar.title: Using 'can't' to express inability
grammar.explanation: We use 'can't' (cannot) to say we are not able to do something. Like 'should', we use the base form of the verb after 'can't'. Unlike Spanish 'no puedo + infinitivo', English 'can't' doesn't need any connector word before the verb.
grammar.rule: After 'can't', use the base form of the verb with no additional words.
grammar.spanishTrap: Some Colombian speakers translate literally from 'no puedo' and forget that 'can't' already includes the negation. Never say 'I no can' or 'I don't can' - it's always 'I can't'.

commonErrors.wrong: I no can go to the party.

commonErrors.why: Use 'can't' for negation, not 'no can'.
Don't use 'to' after 'can't'.

grammar.title: Asking questions with modal verbs
grammar.explanation: To make questions with modal verbs (can, should), we put the modal verb before the subject. The structure is: Modal + subject + base verb + ? Unlike Spanish questions that only need intonation or question marks, English questions with modals require word order change.
grammar.rule: Invert the modal verb and subject to form a question.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers often keep the same word order as statements (¿Tú puedes bailar?) and only change intonation. In English, you must invert: 'Can you dance?' not 'You can dance?'

grammar.title: Modal Verbs: should/shouldn't
grammar.explanation: We use 'should' to give advice or say something is a good idea, and 'shouldn't' for negative advice. Unlike Spanish 'debería', English 'should' is followed directly by the base form of the verb without 'to'. In Spanish you say 'deberías comer', but in English it's 'you should eat' (not 'you should to eat').
grammar.rule: After 'should' and 'shouldn't', always use the base form of the verb (no 'to', no '-ing', no conjugation).
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian Spanish speakers often add 'to' after 'should' because in Spanish we say 'debes de ir' (you should to go), but in English it's just 'you should go' without 'to'.

examples.en: You should rest at home.
examples.es: Deberías descansar en casa.

examples.en: He shouldn't go to work today.
examples.es: Él no debería ir a trabajar hoy.

commonErrors.why: Never use 'to' after 'should'.
Use the base form of the verb after 'should', not the conjugated form.

grammar.title: Feel + Adjective (Describing Emotions)
grammar.explanation: We use 'feel' + adjective to describe emotions or physical sensations. Unlike Spanish where you often use 'estar' (estar triste), in English we use 'feel' (feel sad). The structure is different: in Spanish you say 'estoy feliz' (I am happy), but in English you can say both 'I am happy' or 'I feel happy'.
grammar.rule: Use 'feel' + adjective (not adverb) to express emotions: feel happy, feel sad, feel excited.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian Spanish speakers may confuse 'feel' with 'estar' and try to translate word-for-word. Remember: 'Me siento triste' = 'I feel sad' (not 'I am sad myself').

examples.en: I feel happy today.
examples.es: Me siento feliz hoy.

examples.en: She doesn't feel excited about the trip.
examples.es: Ella no se siente emocionada por el viaje.

commonErrors.why: Use the adjective form, not the adverb, after 'feel'.
Don't add a reflexive pronoun after 'feel' in English.

grammar.rule: After 'can' and 'can't', always use the base form of the verb (no 'to', no '-ing').
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian speakers sometimes confuse 'can' (ability) with 'may' (permission). Also, avoid adding 'to' after 'can' — it's 'I can dance', not 'I can to dance'.

grammar.title: Modal Verb CAN for Ability
grammar.explanation: We use 'can' to express ability or possibility. Unlike Spanish 'poder', 'can' is followed directly by the base form of the verb without 'to'. For example: 'I can swim' (NOT 'I can to swim'). The negative form is 'cannot' or 'can't'.
grammar.rule: After 'can', always use the base form of the verb (infinitive without 'to').

grammar.title: Present Simple with Third Person
grammar.explanation: In present simple, verbs add -s or -es with he, she, it. This is different from Spanish where the verb ending changes for all persons. In English, only third person singular (he/she/it) changes. For example: 'I learn' but 'He learns'.
grammar.rule: Add -s or -es to the verb only when the subject is he, she, it, or a singular noun.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish changes verb endings for all persons (yo aprendo, tú aprendes, él aprende), but English only adds -s for he/she/it. Don't add -s with I, you, we, or they.

grammar.title: There is/There are
grammar.explanation: Use 'There is' for singular nouns and 'There are' for plural nouns to say something exists. Unlike Spanish 'hay' (which doesn't change), English distinguishes between singular and plural. 'There is a book' vs 'There are three books'.
grammar.structure: There is + singular noun / There are + plural noun
grammar.rule: Use 'There is' with one thing and 'There are' with two or more things.
grammar.spanishTrap: In Spanish, 'hay' is the same for singular and plural (hay un libro, hay tres libros). In English, you must change: 'there is' for one, 'there are' for more than one.

grammar.title: Adjectives Before Nouns
grammar.explanation: In English, adjectives always come BEFORE the noun they describe. This is the opposite of Spanish where adjectives usually come after. We say 'a new trick' not 'a trick new'. Adjectives never change form in English (no gender or number agreement).
grammar.rule: Place adjectives directly before the noun, and they never change form.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish says 'un perro viejo' (noun + adjective), but English says 'an old dog' (adjective + noun). Also, English adjectives never change for gender or plural: 'old dog' and 'old dogs' (NOT 'olds dogs').

grammar.title: Modal Verbs: CAN for Ability
grammar.explanation: In English, we use CAN + base verb (infinitive without 'to') to express ability or capacity. Unlike Spanish where you say 'Yo puedo cocinar', in English you NEVER add 'to' after CAN. CAN doesn't change form for different subjects (I can, he can, we can — all the same). The negative is CAN'T or CANNOT.
grammar.rule: After CAN, always use the base form of the verb without 'to'.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian Spanish speakers often say 'I can to cook' because in Spanish you use the infinitive 'cocinar' after 'puedo'. In English, drop the 'to' completely after CAN.

commonErrors.why: Never use 'to' after CAN. Use the base form of the verb.

grammar.title: Gerunds (-ING forms) as Nouns
grammar.explanation: In English, we add -ING to verbs to make them function as nouns (activities or hobbies). This is similar to Spanish infinitives used as nouns. 'Swimming is fun' = 'Nadar es divertido'. Unlike Spanish where you keep the infinitive form, English changes the verb to -ING when it's the subject or object of a sentence.
grammar.rule: When talking about activities as nouns (subjects/objects), use the -ING form, not the infinitive.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers often say 'To swim is fun' (direct translation of 'Nadar es divertido'), but in English we say 'Swimming is fun'. Use -ING, not the infinitive 'to + verb', when the activity is the subject.

commonErrors.why: Use the -ING form when the activity is the subject of the sentence.
After verbs like 'love', 'enjoy', 'like', use -ING for the activity (though 'to draw' is also acceptable after 'love', -ING is more natural).

drillSentences.prompt: To read books helps you learn new vocabulary.

drillSentences.hint: Use -ING form when the activity is the subject

grammar.title: Expressing Opinions with 'In your opinion'
grammar.explanation: To ask for or give opinions in English, we use 'In my/your/his/her opinion' + statement or question. This is similar to Spanish 'En mi/tu opinión'. Note that in English we use possessive adjectives (my, your) not articles (the). Always follow with a complete statement or question.
grammar.rule: Use 'In my/your opinion' followed by a comma, then your statement or question.
grammar.spanishTrap: Some Spanish speakers translate literally 'En la opinión de mí' which sounds unnatural. English uses possessive adjectives directly: 'In MY opinion', not 'In the opinion of me'.

examples.en: In my opinion, practice is most important.
examples.es: En mi opinión, la práctica es más importante.

examples.en: In your opinion, what makes a person successful?
examples.es: En tu opinión, ¿qué hace exitosa a una persona?

commonErrors.wrong: In the opinion of me, motivation is key.
commonErrors.correct: In my opinion, motivation is key.
commonErrors.why: Use the possessive adjective 'my', not 'the opinion of me'.

commonErrors.wrong: In my opinion is important practice a lot.
commonErrors.correct: In my opinion, it is important to practice a lot.
commonErrors.why: You need a complete sentence structure after 'In my opinion'. Include a subject (it) and proper verb form.

drillSentences.prompt: En mi opinión, la tecnología es muy útil para aprender.
drillSentences.answer: In my opinion, technology is very useful for learning.
drillSentences.hint: Remember the comma after 'In my opinion'

drillSentences.prompt: In ___ opinion, what is the best way to study English?
drillSentences.answer: your

drillSentences.prompt: In the opinion of her, coffee is better than tea.
drillSentences.answer: In her opinion, coffee is better than tea.

grammar.title: Present Simple for Habits and Routines
grammar.explanation: We use Present Simple to talk about habits, routines, and things we do regularly (every day, always, usually). Spanish also uses present tense for this, but remember English adds -S to the verb in third person singular (he/she/it). Time expressions like 'every day', 'always', 'usually' are common with this tense.
grammar.structure: Subject + verb (base form) / verb-s (he/she/it) + time expression
grammar.rule: For habits and routines, use Present Simple and add -S to the verb for he/she/it.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian Spanish speakers often forget the -S in third person (saying 'She practice' instead of 'She practices') because Spanish verb endings work differently. Also, frequency adverbs like 'always' go BEFORE the main verb in English, not after like they can in Spanish.

examples.en: I practice cooking every day.
examples.es: Practico cocina cada día.

examples.en: She plays the guitar on weekends.
examples.es: Ella toca la guitarra los fines de semana.

commonErrors.why: Add -S to the verb for he/she/it in Present Simple.

commonErrors.wrong: She cook always dinner at home.
commonErrors.correct: She always cooks dinner at home.
commonErrors.why: Frequency adverbs (always, usually, often) go BEFORE the main verb.

drillSentences.prompt: Mi padre lee el periódico cada mañana.
drillSentences.answer: My father reads the newspaper every morning.

drillSentences.prompt: They ___ soccer on Saturdays.
drillSentences.answer: play

drillSentences.prompt: My teacher explain always the lesson clearly.
drillSentences.answer: My teacher always explains the lesson clearly.
drillSentences.hint: Position of frequency adverbs and third person -S

options: She can to swim very well.
exercises.explanation: After CAN, use the base form of the verb without 'to' and CAN never takes -S.

exercises.question: ___ a new language requires practice and motivation.
exercises.explanation: When an activity is the subject of a sentence, use the -ING form (gerund).

exercises.question: Translate to English: En mi opinión, la motivación es el factor más importante.
exercises.answer: In my opinion, motivation is the most important factor.
exercises.explanation: Use 'In my opinion' followed by a comma, then your statement.

exercises.question: Find and correct the mistake: My brother can to play three musical instruments.
exercises.answer: My brother can play three musical instruments.
exercises.explanation: Never use 'to' after modal verbs like CAN. Use the base form of the verb.

exercises.question: Build a sentence with these words:
What makes a person successful in developing an ability? Choose the INCORRECT answer:
options: Natural ability is the only factor.
All of these factors work together.
exercises.answer: Natural ability is the only factor.
exercises.explanation: Success comes from a combination of motivation, practice, AND natural ability — not just one factor.

exercises.question: My colleague is having ___ writing clearly in English.
exercises.explanation: The phrase 'having difficulty' means experiencing problems with something.

exercises.question: Translate to English: Puedo cocinar bastante bien porque practico cada día.
exercises.answer: I can cook pretty well because I practice every day.
exercises.explanation: Use CAN + base verb for ability, and Present Simple for daily habits.

exercises.question: Which sentence uses the gerund (-ING form) correctly?
options: To draw is her favorite hobby.
exercises.explanation: When an activity is the subject, use the -ING form (gerund), not the infinitive.

exercises.question: Find and correct the mistake: In the opinion of me, swimming is the best exercise.
exercises.answer: In my opinion, swimming is the best exercise.
exercises.explanation: Use the possessive adjective 'my' with 'In my opinion', not 'the opinion of me'.

exercises.question: Give a ___ to show the importance of each factor.
exercises.explanation: A percentage (40%, 50%, etc.) shows how important something is compared to other things.

exercises.question: Build a sentence with these words:
exercises.answer: The advisor can give you good advice.

exercises.question: He ___ the piano every day to improve his skills.
exercises.explanation: For he/she/it in Present Simple, add -S to the verb. This is a daily habit.

exercises.question: Find and correct the mistake: She always cook dinner at home because she enjoys to cook.
exercises.answer: She always cooks dinner at home because she enjoys cooking.
exercises.explanation: Add -S for third person (cooks), and after 'enjoy' use the -ING form (cooking).

speakingPrompts: In your opinion, what is the most important factor for developing a new ability: motivation, practice, or natural ability? Give a percentage to each factor and explain why.

grammar.title: Possessive 's (Saxon Genitive)
grammar.explanation: In English, we use apostrophe + s ('s) to show possession or relationships. Unlike Spanish where we use 'de', in English the possessor comes first. For example, 'el esposo de Kim' becomes 'Kim's husband'.
grammar.rule: Add 's after the person or name to show who owns something or who is related to someone.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian Spanish speakers often translate directly using 'of' (the husband of Kim) instead of the possessive 's (Kim's husband). Remember: in English, the possessor comes BEFORE the thing possessed.

examples.en: Matt is Kim's husband.
examples.es: Matt es el esposo de Kim.

examples.en: Luke is Amy's brother.
examples.es: Luke es el hermano de Amy.

commonErrors.wrong: The car of my father is blue.
commonErrors.why: Use possessive 's, not 'of' for possession.
You must include the apostrophe before the s.

grammar.title: Compound Nouns for Family Relationships (in-law)
grammar.explanation: In English, we create compound words for extended family using hyphens with 'in-law'. Unlike Spanish where each relation has a unique word (suegro, yerno, cuñado), English combines the basic relationship word + 'in-law'. For example, mother-in-law = suegra.
grammar.rule: Use hyphens to connect the words when writing compound family relationship terms with 'in-law'.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian Spanish speakers might forget the hyphens and write 'mother in law' or 'brother in law' as separate words. Always use hyphens: mother-in-law, brother-in-law.

examples.en: Judy is Matt's mother-in-law.
examples.es: Judy es la suegra de Matt.

examples.en: Tom is Kim's brother-in-law.
examples.es: Tom es el cuñado de Kim.

commonErrors.wrong: My sister in law lives in Bogotá.
commonErrors.why: The compound word needs hyphens.

commonErrors.wrong: He is my father in law.
commonErrors.why: Use hyphens to connect the words in compound family terms.

grammar.title: Subject Pronouns and 'to be' for Relationships
grammar.explanation: When describing family relationships, we use subject pronouns (he, she, they) with the correct form of 'to be' (is, are). Unlike Spanish where you can drop the subject pronoun, in English you must always include it. 'Es mi hermano' must be 'He is my brother', not just 'Is my brother'.
grammar.rule: Always include the subject pronoun before the verb 'to be' when describing relationships.
grammar.spanishTrap: In Spanish, you can say 'Es mi tío' without a subject pronoun, but in English you MUST say 'He is my uncle', not 'Is my uncle'. The subject pronoun is mandatory in English.

examples.en: She is my aunt.
examples.es: Ella es mi tía.

examples.en: They are my cousins.
examples.es: Ellos son mis primos.

commonErrors.why: English requires a subject pronoun before the verb.
You must include 'they' as the subject.

grammar.title: Plural Forms of Family Nouns
grammar.explanation: Most family nouns follow regular plural rules (add -s), but some are irregular. 'Child' becomes 'children' (not 'childs'). Unlike Spanish where 'hijos' can mean sons or children, English distinguishes: 'sons' means only males, 'children' means sons and daughters together.
grammar.structure: Regular: noun + s | Irregular: special forms
grammar.rule: Most family words add -s for plural, but 'child → children' is irregular.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian Spanish speakers might say 'childs' instead of 'children'. Also, 'parents' means mother AND father together, not just 'padres' in the sense of priests.

examples.en: My parents are teachers.
examples.es: Mis padres son profesores.

examples.en: Their children are at school.
examples.es: Sus hijos están en la escuela.

commonErrors.why: 'Child' has an irregular plural form.

commonErrors.correct: My parents are doctors. OR My mother is a doctor.
commonErrors.why: 'Parent' is usually used in plural or you specify which parent.

grammar.title: Quantifiers: a lot of, tons of, a bunch of, a few
grammar.explanation: En inglés usamos diferentes cuantificadores para expresar cantidad. A diferencia del español donde 'mucho/muchos' funciona para todo, en inglés hay más variedad. 'A lot of' y 'tons of' significan 'muchos' pero 'tons of' es más informal. 'A bunch of' es muy coloquial y significa 'un grupo de'.
grammar.rule: Use 'a lot of' and 'tons of' with both countable and uncountable nouns in affirmative sentences.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students often translate 'mucho/muchos' as 'much/many' in affirmative sentences. In English, we usually say 'a lot of' or 'tons of' in affirmative sentences, not 'much' or 'many'.

examples.en: I have a lot of cousins in Cali.
examples.es: Tengo muchos primos en Cali.

examples.en: She has tons of homework today.

commonErrors.why: 'Much' is not used with countable nouns in affirmative sentences

commonErrors.why: 'Many' is only for countable nouns; money is uncountable

grammar.title: Phrasal verbs for staying in touch: keep in touch, get together, drop by
grammar.explanation: Los phrasal verbs son verbos seguidos de preposiciones que cambian su significado. 'Keep in touch' significa 'mantener contacto', 'get together' significa 'reunirse', y 'drop by' significa 'pasar por (visitar brevemente)'. En español, estos conceptos son verbos simples o expresiones diferentes.
grammar.rule: Phrasal verbs function as one unit and often cannot be translated word by word from Spanish.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students try to translate literally: 'mantener en contacto' instead of 'keep in touch'. These are fixed expressions that must be learned as complete units.

examples.en: We keep in touch by video call.

grammar.title: Frequency expressions: once a week, every couple of years
grammar.explanation: Para expresar frecuencia en inglés, usamos estructuras como 'once a week', 'twice a month', 'every couple of years'. A diferencia del español, en inglés el artículo 'a' es necesario después de 'once' y 'twice'. 'Every couple of' significa 'cada dos' o 'cada par de'.
grammar.structure: once/twice/three times + a + time period OR every + time period
grammar.rule: Use 'a' (not 'the') after once/twice when talking about frequency per time period.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students often omit the article: 'once week' instead of 'once a week', translating directly from 'una vez semana' without the article that English requires.

examples.en: I visit my grandmother once a week.
examples.es: Visito a mi abuela una vez por semana.

examples.en: We travel to the coast every couple of months.
examples.es: Viajamos a la costa cada dos meses.

commonErrors.correct: I exercise three times a week.
commonErrors.why: Must include 'a' before the time period

commonErrors.wrong: She goes to the gym one time a week.
commonErrors.correct: She goes to the gym once a week.
commonErrors.why: Use 'once' not 'one time' for frequency expressions

drillSentences.prompt: The English club meets ___ ___ week, on Wednesdays at 4 PM.

grammar.title: Describing people with adjectives: outgoing, terrific, young
grammar.explanation: En inglés, los adjetivos siempre van ANTES del sustantivo y nunca cambian su forma (no tienen género ni número). A diferencia del español donde decimos 'extrovertida/extrovertidos', en inglés siempre es 'outgoing' sin importar si es masculino, femenino, singular o plural.
grammar.structure: Subject + be + (super/very/really) + adjective OR Subject + look(s) + adjective
grammar.rule: Adjectives in English do not change form for gender or number and always go before the noun.

grammar.title: Simple Present: Affirmative and Negative Statements
grammar.explanation: In English, the simple present describes habits, facts, and permanent situations. Unlike Spanish, where the verb ending changes for each person (vivo, vives, vive), English only adds '-s' or '-es' for he/she/it. For negatives, we use 'do not' (don't) or 'does not' (doesn't) before the base verb — we NEVER add '-s' to the verb after doesn't.
grammar.structure: Subject + verb (+ -s/-es for he/she/it) OR Subject + don't/doesn't + base verb
grammar.rule: Add -s/-es to verbs with he/she/it in affirmative; use don't/doesn't + base verb for negatives.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students often forget to add -s with he/she/it (saying 'he work' instead of 'he works') or incorrectly add -s after doesn't ('he doesn't works' instead of 'he doesn't work').

examples.en: My in-laws live in Canada.
examples.es: Mis suegros viven en Canadá.

examples.es: Mis primos no trabajan ahora.

examples.es: Mi abuelo no trabaja los fines de semana.

grammar.title: Simple Present: Questions with Do and Does
grammar.explanation: In English, to form yes/no questions in simple present, we use 'Do' or 'Does' at the beginning, followed by the subject and the base verb. Unlike Spanish, where you can just change intonation (¿Tienes hijos?), English requires the auxiliary 'do/does'. Use 'Does' for he/she/it and 'Do' for I/you/we/they.
grammar.rule: Always use the base form of the verb after do/does in questions.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students often add -s to the main verb in questions ('Does he works?') or forget the auxiliary entirely ('You have kids?'). Remember: the -s goes on 'does', not on the main verb.

grammar.title: Contractions: don't and doesn't
grammar.explanation: Contractions combine two words into one shorter form. 'Don't' = 'do not' and 'doesn't' = 'does not'. In spoken English and informal writing, contractions are very common. Spanish doesn't have this type of contraction, so Colombian students must learn when to use each one: 'don't' with I/you/we/they, and 'doesn't' with he/she/it.
grammar.rule: Don't = do not (for I/you/we/they); doesn't = does not (for he/she/it).
grammar.spanishTrap: Students often confuse which contraction to use because Spanish uses 'no' for all persons. Remember: if the subject is he/she/it, use 'doesn't'; for all others, use 'don't'.

grammar.title: Marital Status Adjectives
grammar.explanation: Marital status adjectives describe someone's relationship situation. In English, these are always used with the verb 'to be' (am/is/are), not 'have' like in some Spanish expressions. For example, we say 'She is married' (not 'She has married'). Unlike Spanish, English doesn't require agreement with gender for most of these words (married, single, divorced work for both).
grammar.rule: Use 'to be' (am/is/are) with marital status adjectives, not other verbs.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students might say 'I have married' (influenced by 'estoy casado/tengo pareja'). Always use 'to be': 'I am married'. Also, 'engaged' is a false cognate — it means 'comprometido para casarse', not 'comprometido con una tarea'.

grammar.title: Simple Present Tense - Third Person Singular
grammar.explanation: In the simple present tense, when the subject is he, she, it, or a singular noun, we add -s or -es to the verb. Unlike Spanish, where verb endings change for every person (yo trabajo, tú trabajas, él trabaja), English only changes the verb for third person singular. This is a common error for Spanish speakers who forget to add the -s.
grammar.rule: Add -s to most verbs, -es to verbs ending in -ch, -sh, -ss, -x, -o, and change -y to -ies after a consonant.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers often forget the -s in third person singular because Spanish verb endings are more complex and predictable. For example, saying 'She work' instead of 'She works' because in Spanish we say 'Ella trabaja' where the -a ending is part of the verb conjugation pattern.

examples.en: She lives in Atlanta with her family.
examples.es: Ella vive en Atlanta con su familia.

examples.es: Mi suegro trabaja en un banco.

commonErrors.why: Third person singular (she) needs -s on the verb

grammar.title: Simple Present Tense - Questions with Do/Does
grammar.explanation: To form questions in simple present, we use 'do' or 'does' before the subject, followed by the base form of the verb (without -s). Unlike Spanish, where you can make questions by just changing intonation (¿Vives en Miami?), English requires the auxiliary 'do/does'. Use 'does' for he/she/it and 'do' for I/you/we/they.
grammar.rule: Use 'does' with he/she/it and the base form of the verb (no -s), and 'do' with I/you/we/they.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers often forget to use 'do/does' and say 'You live in Miami?' directly translating from '¿Vives en Miami?'. They also sometimes add -s to the main verb after 'does', saying 'Does she works?' because they think both verbs need the -s.

grammar.title: Simple Present Tense - Negative Statements
grammar.explanation: To form negative statements in simple present, we use 'do not' (don't) or 'does not' (doesn't) before the base form of the verb. Unlike Spanish where you just add 'no' before the conjugated verb (Ella no trabaja), English requires the auxiliary 'do/does' and the main verb must be in base form without -s.
grammar.rule: Use 'doesn't' with he/she/it and 'don't' with I/you/we/they, always followed by the base form of the verb.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers often say 'She no works' or 'He no like' translating directly from Spanish. They also add -s to the verb after 'doesn't', saying 'She doesn't works' because they forget that the auxiliary already shows third person singular.

grammar.title: Responding to Good and Bad News
grammar.explanation: In English, we have specific expressions to respond to good news (That's great! Congratulations! Wonderful!) and bad news (I'm sorry to hear that. That's too bad. Oh, no.). Unlike Spanish, where you might say '¡Qué bueno!' or 'Qué lástima', English has more varied expressions. The possessive 'that's' (that is) is very common in these responses.
grammar.rule: Use positive expressions like 'That's great!' for good news and sympathetic expressions like 'I'm sorry to hear that' for bad news.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers often translate directly from Spanish, saying 'How good!' instead of 'That's great!' or 'What pity!' instead of 'What a pity!' or 'That's too bad'. The structure 'That's + adjective' is very common in English but doesn't have a direct equivalent in Spanish.

examples.en: That's great! Congratulations on your engagement!
examples.es: ¡Qué bien! ¡Felicitaciones por tu compromiso!

examples.en: I'm sorry to hear that. Is she OK?
examples.es: Lamento escuchar eso. ¿Ella está bien?

examples.en: That's wonderful! I'm so happy for you!
examples.es: ¡Qué maravilloso! ¡Estoy muy feliz por ti!

commonErrors.wrong: How good! You are getting married!
commonErrors.correct: That's great! You are getting married!
commonErrors.why: Use 'That's great/wonderful' instead of translating 'Qué bueno' as 'How good'

commonErrors.correct: What a pity about your job. / That's too bad about your job.
commonErrors.why: Need article 'a' before 'pity', or use 'That's too bad' which is more common

grammar.title: Comparative Adjectives: Short Adjectives (+er)
grammar.explanation: En inglés, para comparar usando adjetivos cortos (1-2 sílabas), agregamos -er al final del adjetivo más 'than'. A diferencia del español donde siempre usamos 'más + adjetivo', en inglés los adjetivos cortos cambian su forma. Ejemplos: tall → taller, young → younger, big → bigger.
grammar.structure: Subject + verb + adjective + er + than + object
grammar.rule: Add -er to short adjectives (1-2 syllables) and use 'than' to compare.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students often say 'more tall than' instead of 'taller than' because in Spanish we always use 'más alto que'. Remember: short adjectives use -er, NOT 'more'.

grammar.title: Comparative Adjectives: Long Adjectives (more/less)

grammar.structure: Subject + verb + more/less + adjective + than + object
grammar.rule: Use 'more' or 'less' before long adjectives (2+ syllables) and 'than' after.
grammar.spanishTrap: Students try to add -er to long adjectives like 'intelligenter' or 'expensiver'. If the adjective has 3+ syllables or sounds awkward with -er, use 'more/less' instead.

grammar.title: Irregular Comparative Forms
grammar.explanation: Algunos adjetivos comunes tienen formas comparativas irregulares que debes memorizar. No siguen las reglas de -er o more/less. Los más importantes son: good → better, bad → worse. A diferencia del español donde 'mejor' y 'peor' son regulares, en inglés estas formas cambian completamente.
grammar.structure: Subject + verb + irregular comparative + than + object
grammar.rule: Memorize irregular forms: good → better, bad → worse (NOT gooder or badder).
grammar.spanishTrap: Students say 'more good' or 'more bad' because in Spanish we can say 'más bueno/más malo'. In English, you MUST use 'better' and 'worse' - never 'more good' or 'more bad'.

grammar.title: Comparative Adjectives with 'than'
grammar.explanation: En inglés, para comparar dos personas o cosas, usamos adjetivos comparativos + 'than'. Para adjetivos cortos (1 sílaba), agregamos -er (tall → taller). Para adjetivos largos (2+ sílabas), usamos 'more' + adjetivo (intelligent → more intelligent). Unlike Spanish where you say 'más alto que', English changes the adjective form itself with -er for short words.
grammar.structure: Subject + be + comparative adjective + than + object
grammar.rule: Use -er for short adjectives and 'more' for long adjectives, always followed by 'than'.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students often forget to use 'than' and say 'He is taller his brother' copying Spanish structure 'más alto su hermano'. In English, 'than' is always required.

examples.en: My brother is taller than me.
examples.es: Mi hermano es más alto que yo.

examples.en: She is more intelligent than her classmates.
examples.es: Ella es más inteligente que sus compañeros.

commonErrors.wrong: He is more tall than his sister.
commonErrors.correct: He is taller than his sister.
commonErrors.why: Use -er for one-syllable adjectives, not 'more'.

commonErrors.wrong: My car is faster my friend's car.
commonErrors.correct: My car is faster than my friend's car.
commonErrors.why: Always include 'than' when making comparisons.

grammar.title: Even though (contrast connector)
grammar.explanation: Usamos 'even though' para conectar dos ideas que contrastan o sorprenden. Es similar a 'aunque' en español, pero en inglés siempre va seguido de un sujeto + verbo completo. Unlike Spanish 'aunque', you cannot use 'even though' with just an adjective; you must have a complete clause with subject and verb.
grammar.structure: Even though + subject + verb, main clause
grammar.rule: 'Even though' introduces a contrasting idea and must be followed by a complete clause (subject + verb).
grammar.spanishTrap: Students often write 'Even though young, he is mature' copying Spanish 'aunque joven'. In English you must say 'Even though he is young, he is mature' with the complete verb.

examples.en: Even though I'm the older sibling, he's taller.
examples.es: Aunque soy el hermano mayor, él es más alto.

examples.en: Even though she's busy, she always helps me.
examples.es: Aunque ella está ocupada, siempre me ayuda.

commonErrors.wrong: Even though tired, I went to the gym.

commonErrors.wrong: Although he is young, but he is very responsible.
commonErrors.correct: Although he is young, he is very responsible.
commonErrors.why: Don't use 'but' after 'although/even though'; they already show contrast.

grammar.title: Irregular Comparative Forms
grammar.explanation: Algunos adjetivos tienen formas comparativas irregulares que no siguen las reglas normales. Los más comunes son: good → better (no 'gooder'), bad → worse (no 'badder'), far → farther/further. Estas formas deben memorizarse porque no siguen el patrón -er o 'more'. This is similar to Spanish (bueno → mejor, malo → peor).
grammar.structure: Subject + be + irregular comparative + than + object
grammar.rule: Good becomes 'better', bad becomes 'worse', and far becomes 'farther' in comparatives.
grammar.spanishTrap: Students often say 'more good' or 'more bad' copying the Spanish structure 'más bueno/más malo'. English requires the irregular forms 'better' and 'worse'.

examples.en: She's better at math than me.
examples.es: Ella es mejor en matemáticas que yo.

examples.en: Today's weather is worse than yesterday.
examples.es: El clima de hoy está peor que ayer.

commonErrors.wrong: My grades are more good this year.
commonErrors.correct: My grades are better this year.
commonErrors.why: 'Good' has an irregular comparative form: 'better', not 'more good'.

commonErrors.wrong: His idea is more bad than mine.
commonErrors.correct: His idea is worse than mine.
commonErrors.why: 'Bad' becomes 'worse' in comparatives, not 'more bad'.

drillSentences.answer: My new phone is better than the old one.

grammar.title: Using 'much' and 'a lot' with Comparatives
grammar.explanation: Para enfatizar la diferencia en una comparación, usamos 'much' o 'a lot' antes del adjetivo comparativo. En español usas 'mucho más', pero en inglés 'much' va ANTES del comparativo: 'much taller' (no 'taller much'). 'A lot' es más informal y común en conversación, mientras 'much' es más formal.
grammar.structure: Subject + be + much/a lot + comparative adjective + than + object
grammar.rule: Place 'much' or 'a lot' before the comparative adjective to emphasize the difference.
grammar.spanishTrap: Students often put 'much' after the adjective ('taller much') copying Spanish word order 'más alto mucho'. In English, intensifiers always go BEFORE the comparative.

examples.en: He's much friendlier than before.
examples.es: Él es mucho más amable que antes.

examples.en: She's a lot more intelligent than her brothers.
examples.es: Ella es mucho más inteligente que sus hermanos.

commonErrors.wrong: My brother is taller much than me.
commonErrors.correct: My brother is much taller than me.
commonErrors.why: 'Much' goes before the comparative adjective, not after.

commonErrors.wrong: She is very taller than her sister.
commonErrors.correct: She is much taller than her sister.
commonErrors.why: Use 'much' or 'a lot' with comparatives, not 'very'.

grammar.title: Using 'Both' and 'Neither' for comparisons
grammar.explanation: In English, we use 'both' to talk about two people or things together (ambos/as), and 'neither' to say that something is not true for either of the two (ninguno/a). Unlike Spanish where you might say 'los dos' or 'ni uno ni otro', English has specific words. 'Both' takes a plural verb, while 'neither' takes a singular verb.
grammar.structure: Both + plural noun + plural verb / Neither + singular noun + singular verb
grammar.rule: Both = two things together (plural verb); Neither = not one or the other (singular verb)
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian speakers often use plural verbs with 'neither' because in Spanish 'ninguno de los dos' feels plural. Remember: 'Neither student likes' NOT 'Neither students like'.

examples.en: Both teachers speak English very well.
examples.es: Ambos profesores hablan inglés muy bien.

examples.en: Neither student has a pencil today.
examples.es: Ningún estudiante tiene lápiz hoy.

commonErrors.why: 'Both' needs a plural noun
'Neither' needs a singular noun and singular verb

drillSentences.prompt: Ambas computadoras están apagadas.
drillSentences.answer: Both computers are off.

drillSentences.prompt: I have two dogs but ___ of them likes to swim in the pool.
drillSentences.answer: neither
drillSentences.hint: Use the word that means 'not one or the other'

drillSentences.prompt: Both restaurant serves delicious food.
drillSentences.answer: Both restaurants serve delicious food.
drillSentences.hint: Both needs plural noun and plural verb

grammar.title: Comparative adjectives with 'more' and '-er'
grammar.explanation: English forms comparatives in two ways: short adjectives add -er (tall → taller), while longer adjectives use 'more' (athletic → more athletic). Unlike Spanish where you always use 'más + adjetivo', English changes based on syllable count. Always use 'than' after the comparative form.
grammar.structure: Subject + be + adjective-er / more adjective + than + object
grammar.rule: One-syllable adjectives add -er; two+ syllable adjectives use 'more'
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian speakers often say 'more tall' or 'more short' because Spanish uses 'más alto/bajo' for everything. English only uses 'more' with longer adjectives like 'athletic', 'expensive', 'difficult'.

examples.en: He is taller than his brother.
examples.es: Él es más alto que su hermano.

examples.en: She is more athletic than me.
examples.es: Ella es más atlética que yo.

commonErrors.wrong: My house is more big than yours.
commonErrors.correct: My house is bigger than yours.
commonErrors.why: 'Big' is one syllable, so it needs -er not 'more'

commonErrors.wrong: This test is difficulter than the last one.
commonErrors.correct: This test is more difficult than the last one.
commonErrors.why: 'Difficult' has three syllables, so it needs 'more' not -er

drillSentences.prompt: Mi celular es más caro que el tuyo.
drillSentences.answer: My phone is more expensive than yours.

drillSentences.prompt: My grandmother cooks better ___ any restaurant chef. Her meals are always delicious.
drillSentences.answer: than
drillSentences.hint: Use the word that connects two parts of a comparison

drillSentences.prompt: Learning guitar is more easy than learning piano.
drillSentences.answer: Learning guitar is easier than learning piano.
drillSentences.hint: Easy is a two-syllable adjective ending in -y

grammar.title: Present Simple: Third Person -s
grammar.explanation: In English present simple, verbs with he/she/it add -s or -es at the end. This is different from Spanish where the verb ending changes for all persons (yo hablo, tú hablas, él habla). In English, only third person singular is different. Remember: he likes, she tends, it has.
grammar.rule: Add -s to most verbs, -es to verbs ending in s/sh/ch/x/o with he/she/it
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian speakers often forget the -s because in Spanish 'él habla' and 'ellos hablan' both end differently but the verb changes throughout. English only adds -s for he/she/it: 'He speak' is WRONG, must be 'He speaks'.

examples.en: She tends to be quiet in class.
examples.es: Ella tiende a ser callada en clase.

examples.en: He prefers jazz music.
examples.es: Él prefiere música jazz.

commonErrors.wrong: My mother work in a hospital.
commonErrors.correct: My mother works in a hospital.
commonErrors.why: 'Mother' is third person singular (she), so the verb needs -s
Third person negative uses 'doesn't' not 'don't'

drillSentences.prompt: Mi papá cocina muy bien los domingos.
drillSentences.answer: My dad cooks very well on Sundays.

drillSentences.prompt: My little sister ___ to school every day by bus. She never walks.
drillSentences.answer: goes

drillSentences.prompt: The teacher teach mathematics and science.
drillSentences.answer: The teacher teaches mathematics and science.
drillSentences.hint: Add -es to verbs ending in -ch with he/she/it

grammar.title: Verb 'look' + adjective vs 'look like' + noun
grammar.explanation: In English, 'look' + adjective describes appearance or state (look happy, look tired), while 'look like' + noun makes comparisons (look like twins, look like my father). Spanish uses 'verse' for both but English distinguishes them. This is important when describing similarities between people.
grammar.structure: Subject + look + adjective / Subject + look like + noun
grammar.rule: Use 'look' + adjective to describe; use 'look like' + noun to compare
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian speakers often say 'they look as twins' or 'she looks as her mother' translating 'como' directly. English uses 'like' not 'as' in this pattern: 'look like twins' not 'look as twins'.

examples.en: They look identical.
examples.es: Se ven idénticos.

examples.en: She looks like her sister.
examples.es: Ella se parece a su hermana.

commonErrors.why: Use 'like' not 'as' after 'look' when comparing to a noun
'Tired' is an adjective, so use 'look' without 'like'

drillSentences.prompt: Esa casa se parece a un castillo.
drillSentences.answer: That house looks like a castle.

drillSentences.prompt: My new classmate ___ very friendly and intelligent. I want to talk to her.
drillSentences.answer: looks

drillSentences.prompt: This pizza looks as the one from that restaurant downtown.
drillSentences.answer: This pizza looks like the one from that restaurant downtown.
drillSentences.hint: Use 'like' not 'as' when comparing with a noun

exercises.question: Which sentence is grammatically INCORRECT?
exercises.explanation: 'Neither' requires a singular verb, so it should be 'Neither teacher likes coffee.'

exercises.question: My two younger sisters, Ana and Sofia, ___ in the park every Saturday morning. They never miss their routine.
exercises.explanation: The subject 'sisters' is plural, so we use the base form 'run' without -s.

exercises.question: Translate to English: Mi hermano mayor es más tímido que yo.
exercises.answer: My older brother is shyer than me.
exercises.explanation: 'Shy' becomes 'shyer' in the comparative form (change y to i and add -er).

exercises.question: Build a sentence with these words:
exercises.answer: Both girls have the same birthday.

exercises.question: Find and correct the mistake: She look like very intelligent.
exercises.explanation: Use 'look' + adjective without 'like'. Also, third person needs 'looks' not 'look'.

exercises.question: Complete: ___ of my parents speak English fluently.
exercises.explanation: 'Both' is correct because we're talking about two parents who speak English.

exercises.question: My best friend's personality is very different ___ mine. She is outgoing and I am quiet.
exercises.explanation: We use 'different from' to show contrast between two things.

exercises.question: Match each word with its translation
exercises.explanation: All matches are correct.

exercises.question: Which comparative form is CORRECT?
exercises.explanation: 'Athletic' has three syllables, so it uses 'more' not -er.

exercises.question: Translate to English: Ningún estudiante tiene tarea hoy.
exercises.explanation: 'Neither' takes a singular noun and singular verb form.

exercises.question: He ___ to be quiet when he is with larger groups of people. In small groups, he talks more.
exercises.explanation: Third person singular 'he' requires 'tends' (with -s) in present simple.

exercises.question: Build a sentence with these words:
exercises.answer: They look identical but have different personalities.

exercises.question: Find and correct the mistake: My sister is more quiet than my brother.
exercises.answer: My sister is quieter than my brother.
exercises.explanation: 'Quiet' is a short adjective (two syllables), so it uses -er not 'more'.

exercises.question: What does 'tell apart' mean?
exercises.explanation: 'Tell apart' means to be able to see the difference between two similar things or people.

grammar.title: Third Person Singular Verbs (does/has)
grammar.explanation: In English, when we use he, she, or it, we must add -s or -es to the verb. For questions and negatives with he/she/it, we use 'does' (not 'do') and the base verb without -s. This is different from Spanish where the verb ending changes but question formation is simpler.
grammar.rule: Always use 'does' for questions and negatives with he, she, or it, and keep the main verb in base form.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian Spanish speakers often forget the -s ending or incorrectly use 'do' instead of 'does' because Spanish verb conjugation doesn't follow this pattern (él tiene vs. he has).

examples.en: Does she have any cousins?
examples.es: ¿Ella tiene primos?

examples.en: Where does he live?
examples.es: ¿Dónde vive él?

commonErrors.why: After 'does', use the base form without -s
Use 'does' (not 'do') with he, she, or it

drillSentences.prompt: ¿Tu mamá cocina comida colombiana?
drillSentences.answer: Does your mom cook Colombian food?
drillSentences.hint: Remember to use 'does' for questions with she

drillSentences.prompt: My teacher ___ three languages. She speaks English, Spanish, and French at home.
drillSentences.answer: speaks

drillSentences.prompt: My little brother do his homework every afternoon.
drillSentences.answer: My little brother does his homework every afternoon.

grammar.title: Linking of Sounds in Questions
grammar.explanation: In spoken English, words connect smoothly when one word ends with a consonant sound and the next begins with a vowel sound. For example, 'does_he' sounds like /dʌzi/. This linking makes English sound natural and fluent, unlike Spanish where words are typically pronounced more separately.
grammar.structure: Final consonant + initial vowel = linked sound
grammar.rule: Connect the final consonant of one word to the vowel sound at the beginning of the next word.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers often pause between words instead of linking them, which sounds choppy in English. Practice connecting 'does_he', 'does_she', 'has_any' as single sound units.

examples.en: Does she /dʌʃi/ have cousins?
examples.es: ¿Ella tiene primos? (con sonidos conectados)

examples.en: How many /haʊˈmeni/ cousins?
examples.es: ¿Cuántos primos? (con sonidos conectados)

commonErrors.why: Words should flow together, not be separated
Link 'does' and 'he' without pausing

drillSentences.prompt: ¿Cuántos años tiene tu perro? (conecta los sonidos)
drillSentences.answer: How old is your dog?

drillSentences.prompt: Practice linking: Can___ eat pizza? My friend wants to know because she is vegetarian.
drillSentences.answer: he

drillSentences.prompt: What. Is. Your. Name? (pronounced with pauses between each word)
drillSentences.answer: What_is your name? (linked smoothly)
drillSentences.hint: Words should connect in natural speech

grammar.title: Similarity and Difference Expressions
grammar.explanation: To compare people or things, use 'similar to' (parecido a) and 'different from' (diferente de). English requires the prepositions 'to' after 'similar' and 'from' after 'different'. You can also say 'the same as' (igual que) or 'both' (ambos) to show similarities.
grammar.structure: Subject + is/are + similar to / different from + object
grammar.rule: Use 'similar to' and 'different from' (never 'similar as' or 'different than' in formal English).
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish uses 'parecido a' and 'diferente de', but Colombian speakers might incorrectly translate 'similar as' or 'different of' directly from Spanish patterns.

examples.en: My brother is similar to my father.
examples.es: Mi hermano es parecido a mi padre.

examples.en: Their personalities are different from each other.
examples.es: Sus personalidades son diferentes entre sí.

commonErrors.wrong: He is similar as his brother.
commonErrors.correct: He is similar to his brother.
commonErrors.why: Use 'to' after 'similar', not 'as'

commonErrors.wrong: She is different of her sister.
commonErrors.correct: She is different from her sister.
commonErrors.why: Use 'from' after 'different', not 'of'

drillSentences.prompt: El clima de Bogotá es diferente del clima de Cartagena.
drillSentences.answer: The weather in Bogotá is different from the weather in Cartagena.

drillSentences.prompt: My new school is similar ___ my old school. Both schools have a big library and many computers.
drillSentences.answer: to

drillSentences.prompt: This book is different than that movie.
drillSentences.answer: This book is different from that movie.

grammar.title: Possessive Adjectives (my, your, his, her)
grammar.explanation: Possessive adjectives show ownership and always go before the noun. Unlike Spanish, English possessive adjectives don't change based on whether the noun is masculine, feminine, or plural. 'His' is for male owners, 'her' is for female owners, and they stay the same regardless of what is owned.
grammar.rule: The possessive adjective never changes form - it's always the same whether the thing owned is singular, plural, masculine, or feminine.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers might say 'his sister' and 'his sisters' correctly but get confused with 'su' translating to both 'his' and 'her' in Spanish. Remember: 'his' = él, 'her' = ella, regardless of what follows.

examples.en: My brother-in-law is married to my sister.
examples.es: Mi cuñado está casado con mi hermana.

examples.en: Her personality is very friendly.
examples.es: Su personalidad es muy amigable.

commonErrors.why: Use 'his' (possessive), not 'he' (subject pronoun)
Use 'her' (possessive), not 'she' (subject pronoun)

drillSentences.prompt: Mi profesor estudia en su oficina todos los días.
drillSentences.answer: My teacher studies in his office every day.
drillSentences.hint: Choose 'his' or 'her' based on teacher's gender

drillSentences.prompt: ___ computer is broken. She can't do her homework now because it doesn't turn on.
drillSentences.answer: Her

drillSentences.prompt: They house is very big and beautiful.
drillSentences.answer: Their house is very big and beautiful.

exercises.question: Which sentence is CORRECT?
exercises.explanation: With 'does', use the base form 'have' (not 'has').

exercises.question: My cousin is very ___. She loves playing soccer, basketball, and running every morning.
exercises.explanation: Athletic describes someone who is good at sports and physical activities.

exercises.question: Translate to English: Mi hermana es tímida pero muy amigable.
exercises.answer: My sister is shy but very friendly.
exercises.explanation: Shy = tímida, friendly = amigable, but = pero.

exercises.question: Find and correct the mistake: My brother-in-law are an engineer.
exercises.explanation: Use 'is' (singular) with 'brother-in-law', not 'are' (plural).

exercises.question: Build a sentence with these words:
Which word means 'cuñado' in English?
exercises.explanation: Brother-in-law is your sister's husband or your spouse's brother.

exercises.question: How many ___ does she have? She told me she has four from her mother's side and three from her father's side.
exercises.explanation: Cousins = primos/primas. Use plural because 'how many' asks about multiple people.

exercises.question: Complete the sentence: They are ___ in some ways but ___ in others.
exercises.explanation: Similar and different are adjectives used to compare things.

exercises.question: Find and correct the mistake: She personality is very outgoing and friendly.
exercises.answer: Her personality is very outgoing and friendly.
exercises.explanation: Use 'her' (possessive adjective), not 'she' (subject pronoun) before a noun.

exercises.question: Translate to English: ¿Dónde vive tu primo?
exercises.explanation: Use 'does' with he/she/it in questions, and 'cousin' for primo.

exercises.question: My father has a ___ and a ___. He looks like a traditional Colombian grandfather with his facial hair.
exercises.explanation: Mustache = bigote, beard = barba. Both are facial hair.

exercises.question: Build a sentence with these words:
Which adjective describes someone who works a lot and studies hard?
exercises.explanation: Hard-working = trabajador/a, someone who puts in a lot of effort.

exercises.question: Find and correct the mistake: He is similar as his father.
exercises.answer: He is similar to his father.
exercises.explanation: Use 'similar to', not 'similar as'. The correct preposition is 'to'.

speakingPrompts: Describe two people in your family. Talk about their appearance, personality, and what they do.

Tell me about your relatives. Who is the most outgoing person? Who is the most hard-working?
Practice asking and answering: 'Does your brother/sister/cousin live near you? What does he/she do?'

grammar.title: Present Simple: Third Person Singular
grammar.explanation: In English, when we talk about he, she, or it in present tense, we add -s or -es to the verb. This is different from Spanish where the verb ending changes more. Example: 'He lives' (él vive) - the verb 'live' becomes 'lives'. This happens with all verbs except modals.
grammar.rule: Add -s or -es to verbs after he, she, it, or singular nouns in present simple.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers often forget the -s ending because in Spanish the conjugation is more obvious in the verb form itself. In English, YOU MUST add -s even though it seems small.

examples.en: She helps with household chores.
examples.es: Ella ayuda con las tareas domésticas.

examples.en: My father calls me every day.
examples.es: Mi padre me llama todos los días.

commonErrors.why: Must add -s to the verb after 'he'
Singular subjects need verb + -s

drillSentences.prompt: Mi hermana estudia inglés todos los días.
drillSentences.answer: My sister studies English every day.
drillSentences.hint: Remember to add -s to the verb

drillSentences.prompt: My teacher always ___ us interesting stories about his travels. He talks about different countries every week.
drillSentences.answer: tells

drillSentences.prompt: My dog run very fast in the park.
drillSentences.answer: My dog runs very fast in the park.

grammar.title: Frequency Expressions
grammar.explanation: We use expressions like 'every day', 'once a month', 'at least' to say how often something happens. Unlike Spanish where 'cada día' comes flexibly in the sentence, English frequency expressions have specific positions: usually at the end of the sentence or after the subject.
grammar.rule: Frequency expressions usually go at the end of the sentence.
grammar.spanishTrap: In Spanish you can say 'cada día yo llamo' but in English we say 'I call every day' - the frequency comes AFTER the verb and object, not at the beginning.

examples.en: He calls his kids every day.
examples.es: Él llama a sus hijos todos los días.

examples.en: She visits her house once a month.
examples.es: Ella visita su casa una vez al mes.

commonErrors.wrong: Every day I go to the school.
commonErrors.correct: I go to school every day.
commonErrors.why: Frequency expression goes at the end
Put frequency after the verb

drillSentences.prompt: Nosotros comemos pizza dos veces al mes.
drillSentences.answer: We eat pizza twice a month.

drillSentences.prompt: My brother plays soccer ___. He has practice on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays.
drillSentences.answer: three times a week

drillSentences.prompt: Always my mom cooks dinner at 7 PM.
drillSentences.answer: My mom always cooks dinner at 7 PM.

grammar.title: Quantifiers with 'of'
grammar.explanation: We use expressions like 'about 20%', 'two-thirds', 'at least 30' to talk about amounts. These need 'of' before 'the' or possessive words. This is similar to Spanish 'de' but English requires both 'of' AND 'the': 'two-thirds of the children' (dos tercios de los niños).
grammar.rule: After quantifiers like fractions and percentages, use 'of' before the noun group.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers sometimes forget 'the' after 'of'. You need both: 'About 70% of THE households' not 'About 70% of households'. The 'the' is required when talking about a specific group.

examples.en: About 70% of the households are multi-generational.
examples.es: Aproximadamente el 70% de los hogares son multigeneracionales.

examples.en: Two-thirds of all children live with a single parent.
examples.es: Dos tercios de todos los niños viven con un padre soltero.

commonErrors.correct: About 50% of the students study English.
commonErrors.why: Need 'of the' after percentages

commonErrors.correct: One-third of the children are young.
commonErrors.why: Need 'the' and verb agrees with plural noun

drillSentences.prompt: La mitad de mis amigos juegan videojuegos.
drillSentences.answer: Half of my friends play video games.

drillSentences.prompt: About 80% ___ people in my city use smartphones. This number is very high compared to ten years ago.
drillSentences.answer: of the

drillSentences.prompt: One-fourth of students in my class speaks French.
drillSentences.answer: One-fourth of the students in my class speak French.

grammar.title: Possessive Forms with Family
grammar.explanation: We show possession with 's (apostrophe s) for people: 'Wu's ex-husband', 'my mother's house'. This is different from Spanish 'de': instead of 'el esposo de Wu' we say 'Wu's husband'. The 's comes directly after the person's name or the family member word.
grammar.rule: Add 's after a person or family word to show possession.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers want to say 'the house of my mother' (like 'la casa de mi madre'), but English says 'my mother's house'. The possessor comes FIRST, then 's, then the thing.

examples.en: Wu's ex-husband visits their kids.
examples.es: El exesposo de Wu visita a sus hijos.

examples.en: My grandmother's house is very big.
examples.es: La casa de mi abuela es muy grande.

commonErrors.wrong: The car of my father is new.
commonErrors.why: Use 's for people, not 'of'
Need apostrophe + s

drillSentences.prompt: El teléfono de mi hermano es nuevo.
drillSentences.answer: My brother's phone is new.

drillSentences.prompt: My ___ restaurant is very popular in Bogotá. She opened it three years ago and now it has many customers.
drillSentences.answer: aunt's

drillSentences.prompt: The bicycle of Carlos is blue.
drillSentences.answer: Carlos's bicycle is blue.

exercises.question: What does 'multi-generational household' mean?
options: Only parents and children live together
Grandparents, parents, and children live together
Only grandparents live in the house
exercises.answer: Grandparents, parents, and children live together
exercises.explanation: Multi-generational means multiple generations (grandparents, parents, children) live in one house.

exercises.question: Complete: My grandmother has three ___. They are my brother, my cousin, and me.
exercises.explanation: Grandchildren are the children of your children (nietos).

exercises.question: Translate to English: Mi madre ayuda con las tareas domésticas todos los días.

grammar.title: Present Simple: Questions with 'Do/Does'
grammar.explanation: In English, we form questions in the present simple with 'do' or 'does' before the subject. Unlike Spanish where you can make questions by changing intonation (¿Vives aquí?), English requires the auxiliary: 'Do you live here?' Use 'do' with I/you/we/they and 'does' with he/she/it. The main verb stays in base form after do/does.
grammar.rule: Questions in present simple require 'do/does' + subject + base verb (no -s ending on the main verb).
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students often forget 'do/does' and try to form questions like Spanish by changing word order or intonation: 'You know anyone?' instead of 'Do you know anyone?' Remember: English needs the auxiliary.

examples.en: Do you know anyone who lives in a multi-generational household?
examples.es: ¿Conoces a alguien que viva en un hogar multigeneracional?

examples.en: Does she live with her parents?
examples.es: ¿Ella vive con sus padres?

commonErrors.correct: Do you live with your family?
commonErrors.why: Questions need the auxiliary 'do' before the subject.
After 'does', use the base form of the verb (no -s ending).

grammar.title: Frequency Adverbs: 'Usually' and 'Extremely'
grammar.explanation: Frequency adverbs (usually, always, often, never) typically go BEFORE the main verb in English, but AFTER the verb 'to be'. This is different from Spanish where adverbs are more flexible. Degree adverbs like 'extremely' modify adjectives and go BEFORE the adjective they describe.
grammar.structure: Subject + frequency adverb + main verb OR Subject + be + frequency adverb
grammar.rule: Frequency adverbs go before main verbs but after 'be'. Degree adverbs go before adjectives.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers often put frequency adverbs at the end like in Spanish (Voy al gimnasio usualmente → I go to the gym usually). In English, it should be: 'I usually go to the gym.' Don't translate word-for-word.

examples.en: Children usually leave home between 21 and 25.
examples.es: Los niños usualmente se van de casa entre los 21 y 25 años.

examples.en: They're extremely unusual in our country.
examples.es: Son extremadamente inusuales en nuestro país.

commonErrors.wrong: I go usually to school by bus.
commonErrors.correct: I usually go to school by bus.
commonErrors.why: Frequency adverbs go before the main verb, not after.
Degree adverbs like 'extremely' go before the adjective.

drillSentences.prompt: Mi mamá siempre prepara el desayuno a las seis de la mañana.

grammar.title: Present Simple: Negative Statements
grammar.explanation: To make negative sentences in present simple, use 'don't' (do not) or 'doesn't' (does not) before the base verb. Unlike Spanish where you add 'no' before the conjugated verb (No vivo aquí), English uses the auxiliary don't/doesn't and the verb stays in base form. Use 'don't' with I/you/we/they and 'doesn't' with he/she/it.
grammar.rule: Negative present simple: subject + don't/doesn't + base verb (no -s ending on main verb).
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students often say 'He no lives here' copying Spanish structure, or 'He doesn't lives' adding -s incorrectly. Remember: after doesn't/don't, the verb is ALWAYS in base form without -s.

examples.en: They don't want to continue living with their parents.
examples.es: No quieren continuar viviendo con sus padres.

examples.en: She doesn't know anyone in that building.
examples.es: Ella no conoce a nadie en ese edificio.

commonErrors.wrong: He doesn't wants to leave home.
commonErrors.correct: He doesn't want to leave home.
commonErrors.why: After 'doesn't', use the base form without -s.
English uses 'don't/doesn't', not 'no' for negatives in present simple.

drillSentences.prompt: Mi hermano no come carne porque es vegetariano.
drillSentences.answer: My brother doesn't eat meat because he is vegetarian.

drillSentences.prompt: We ___ have time to watch television tonight. We need to finish our homework first.
