grammar.title: Articles: 'A' vs 'The' with Singular Nouns
grammar.explanation: Use 'a' when mentioning something for the first time or when it's not specific (any one). Use 'the' when referring to something specific or already mentioned. Spanish has similar rules but English uses articles more strictly. Unlike Spanish where you can omit articles in some cases (Tengo trabajo), English requires them (I have a job, not I have job).
grammar.structure: a/an + singular countable noun (first mention) | the + singular/plural noun (specific)
grammar.rule: Use 'a/an' for non-specific singular nouns; use 'the' for specific nouns or second mentions.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers often drop articles where English requires them. 'She needs job' is wrong; it must be 'She needs a job.' Also, Spanish uses articles with abstract nouns more freely (La vida es bella) while English often doesn't (Life is beautiful, not The life).

examples.en: They get a job after finishing school.
examples.es: Consiguen un trabajo después de terminar la escuela.

examples.en: Complete the survey about your household.
examples.es: Completa la encuesta sobre tu hogar.

commonErrors.wrong: I need job to pay for university.
commonErrors.correct: I need a job to pay for university.
commonErrors.why: 'Job' is a countable singular noun and needs an article.

commonErrors.wrong: She lives in house with her parents.
commonErrors.correct: She lives in a house with her parents.
commonErrors.why: First mention of a countable noun needs 'a' or 'an'.

grammar.title: Possessive 's with family relationships
grammar.explanation: In English, we use 's after a person's name to show possession or relationship (Kim's husband, Luke's sister). Unlike Spanish where we use 'de' (el esposo de Kim), English places the possessor BEFORE what they possess. This is called the possessive case.
grammar.rule: Add 's after the person's name to show who someone belongs to or is related to.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students often say 'the husband of Kim' (direct translation from 'el esposo de Kim'), but English requires 'Kim's husband'. The possessor comes FIRST in English.

examples.en: Matt is Kim's husband.
examples.es: Matt es el esposo de Kim.

examples.en: Luke and Amy are Kim's children.
examples.es: Luke y Amy son los hijos de Kim.

commonErrors.wrong: The mother of Sara is a teacher.
commonErrors.why: Use possessive 's, not 'of' for people and family relationships.
The apostrophe 's shows possession, not plural. For plural, just add 's'.

grammar.title: Subject pronouns with the verb 'to be'
grammar.explanation: Subject pronouns (I, you, he, she, it, we, they) come before the verb 'to be' (am, is, are). Unlike Spanish where you can say just 'es' or 'son', English ALWAYS needs a subject pronoun before the verb. You cannot drop the pronoun.
grammar.rule: Always use a subject pronoun before 'am', 'is', or 'are' - never drop it like in Spanish.
grammar.spanishTrap: In Spanish you can say 'Es mi hermano' without a pronoun, but in English you MUST say 'He is my brother'. Never drop the subject pronoun.

examples.en: She is Kim's sister.
examples.es: Ella es la hermana de Kim.

examples.en: They are Luke and Amy's grandparents.
examples.es: Ellos son los abuelos de Luke y Amy.

commonErrors.why: English always requires a subject pronoun before the verb 'to be'.

commonErrors.correct: They are students in my class.
commonErrors.why: You cannot drop the subject pronoun 'they' in English.

grammar.title: Compound family relationship nouns with hyphens
grammar.explanation: Family relationships with 'in-law' are written with hyphens (mother-in-law, sister-in-law, brother-in-law). These are compound nouns that describe relationships through marriage. Unlike Spanish which uses separate words (suegra, cuñada), English connects them with hyphens.
grammar.rule: Always use hyphens to connect 'in-law' relationships: mother-in-law, father-in-law, sister-in-law, etc.
grammar.spanishTrap: Students often write 'mother in law' or 'motherinlaw', but the correct form always uses TWO hyphens: 'mother-in-law'.

examples.en: My mother-in-law is very friendly.
examples.es: Mi suegra es muy amable.

examples.en: His brother-in-law works in Bogotá.
examples.es: Su cuñado trabaja en Bogotá.

commonErrors.wrong: My sister in law lives in Cali.
commonErrors.why: Compound family relationships with 'in-law' need hyphens.

commonErrors.wrong: They are my parents in laws.
commonErrors.why: The plural 's' goes at the end, after the second hyphen.

grammar.title: Expressions of Quantity with 'of'
grammar.explanation: In English, we use phrases like 'a lot of', 'tons of', 'a bunch of' to describe large quantities. Unlike Spanish where you might say 'muchos primos', English requires the preposition 'of' after these quantity expressions. The pattern is always: quantity expression + of + plural noun.
grammar.structure: tons of / a lot of / a bunch of + plural noun
grammar.rule: After quantity expressions ending in 'of', always use a plural noun.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students often forget the 'of' and say 'tons cousins' instead of 'tons of cousins', directly translating from 'montones primos' in Spanish.

examples.en: I have tons of cousins.
examples.es: Tengo montones de primos.

examples.en: A bunch of us get together every month.
examples.es: Un montón de nosotros nos reunimos cada mes.

commonErrors.wrong: I have tons cousins in my family.
commonErrors.correct: I have tons of cousins in my family.
commonErrors.why: You must include 'of' after quantity expressions like 'tons', 'a lot', 'a bunch'.

commonErrors.wrong: She has a lot friend at school.
commonErrors.correct: She has a lot of friends at school.
commonErrors.why: After 'a lot', you need 'of' plus a plural noun.

drillSentences.prompt: Mi hermana tiene montones de libros en su habitación.
drillSentences.answer: My sister has tons of books in her room.

drillSentences.prompt: There are a bunch ___ students waiting outside the classroom. The teacher will arrive soon.

grammar.title: Phrasal Verbs for Social Interaction
grammar.explanation: English uses many phrasal verbs (verb + preposition/adverb) to describe social activities. 'Get together' means to meet, 'keep in touch' means to maintain contact, and 'drop by' means to visit briefly. Unlike Spanish verbs which are often single words, these English phrases cannot be separated or translated word-by-word.
grammar.rule: Phrasal verbs like 'get together', 'keep in touch', and 'drop by' function as single units and have specific meanings different from their individual words.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students often try to translate word-by-word, saying 'We join together' instead of 'We get together', or 'I pass by' instead of 'I drop by'.

examples.en: We get together once a month.
examples.es: Nos reunimos una vez al mes.

examples.en: I drop by to say hello every week.
examples.es: Paso a saludar cada semana.

commonErrors.wrong: Do you maintain in touch with your cousins?
commonErrors.correct: Do you keep in touch with your cousins?
commonErrors.why: 'Keep in touch' is the correct phrasal verb; 'maintain' alone doesn't work in English for this meaning.

commonErrors.wrong: I pass by her house yesterday.
commonErrors.correct: I dropped by her house yesterday.
commonErrors.why: 'Drop by' is the phrasal verb for visiting briefly; 'pass by' means to go past without stopping.

drillSentences.prompt: ¿Te mantienes en contacto con tus amigos de la universidad?
drillSentences.answer: Do you keep in touch with your friends from university?

drillSentences.prompt: My friends and I ___ together every Friday to play football. We meet at the park at 5 pm.

drillSentences.answer: I will drop by your office tomorrow to give you the documents.

grammar.title: Present Simple with Frequency Adverbs
grammar.explanation: English uses frequency adverbs like 'once', 'every couple of', 'every week' to describe how often actions happen. These usually come at the END of the sentence, unlike Spanish where they can appear in different positions. The structure is: subject + verb + object + frequency expression.
grammar.rule: Frequency expressions usually come at the end of the sentence in English.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students often place frequency expressions at the beginning of sentences (like in Spanish 'Una vez a la semana visito...'), but in English it's more natural to say 'I visit... once a week.'

examples.en: I drop by to say hello once a week.
examples.es: Paso a saludar una vez por semana.

examples.en: We get together once every couple of weeks.
examples.es: Nos reunimos una vez cada dos semanas.

commonErrors.wrong: Once a week I visit my grandmother.
commonErrors.correct: I visit my grandmother once a week.
commonErrors.why: In English, frequency expressions usually go at the end of the sentence, not at the beginning.

commonErrors.wrong: Every month we together get at my house.
commonErrors.correct: We get together at my house every month.
commonErrors.why: The frequency expression 'every month' comes at the end, and phrasal verbs stay together.

grammar.title: Comparative Adjectives
grammar.explanation: To compare two things in English, we add '-er' to short adjectives (young → younger) or use 'more' with longer adjectives (outgoing → more outgoing). Unlike Spanish where you use 'más' for all adjectives, English has two different patterns depending on the adjective length.
grammar.structure: subject + verb + adjective-er + than / more + adjective + than
grammar.rule: One-syllable adjectives add '-er'; adjectives with two or more syllables usually use 'more'.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students often say 'more young' instead of 'younger' because Spanish uses 'más joven' for all comparatives.

examples.en: She looks much younger than her age.
examples.es: Ella se ve mucho más joven que su edad.

examples.en: She's more outgoing than me.
examples.es: Ella es más extrovertida que yo.

commonErrors.wrong: My sister is more young than my brother.
commonErrors.correct: My sister is younger than my brother.
commonErrors.why: Short adjectives like 'young' add '-er', not 'more'.

commonErrors.wrong: He is more tall than his father.
commonErrors.correct: He is taller than his father.
commonErrors.why: One-syllable adjectives like 'tall' take '-er', not 'more'.

grammar.title: Simple Present Tense: Affirmative and Negative
grammar.explanation: The simple present tense describes habits, facts, and general truths. Unlike Spanish, English requires the auxiliary 'do/does' for negatives and questions. For negatives, use 'don't' (do not) with I/you/we/they and 'doesn't' (does not) with he/she/it. The main verb stays in base form after 'don't/doesn't'.
grammar.rule: Use don't/doesn't + base verb for negatives; add -s/-es to verbs with he/she/it in affirmatives.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian Spanish speakers often forget 'doesn't' and say 'My aunt don't live nearby' instead of 'My aunt doesn't live nearby'. Remember: he/she/it needs 'doesn't', not 'don't'.

examples.en: My in-laws live in Canada.

examples.es: Mi abuela no trabaja los fines de semana.

commonErrors.why: Use 'doesn't' (not 'don't') with he/she/it
After 'doesn't', use the base form of the verb (no -s)

grammar.title: Simple Present Tense: Questions with Do/Does
grammar.explanation: To form yes/no questions in simple present, use 'Do/Does + subject + base verb'. Use 'Do' with I/you/we/they and 'Does' with he/she/it. Unlike Spanish, you cannot just change intonation; you must use the auxiliary 'do/does'. The main verb stays in base form (no -s).
grammar.rule: Always use 'do/does' to form questions in simple present; the main verb is always in base form.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers often forget the auxiliary and say 'You have kids?' instead of 'Do you have kids?'. In English, the auxiliary 'do/does' is mandatory for questions.

examples.en: Do you have kids? Yes, I do.
examples.es: ¿Tienes hijos? Sí, los tengo.

examples.en: Where do your in-laws live?

commonErrors.why: After 'does', use the base form 'have' (not 'has')

grammar.title: Contractions with Be and Do
grammar.explanation: Contractions combine two words into one shorter form. In English, we use contractions in spoken and informal written English. 'Don't' = do not, 'doesn't' = does not. Unlike Spanish, which has very few contractions, English uses them constantly in conversation.
grammar.rule: Use contractions in informal speech and writing; they make your English sound more natural.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers sometimes confuse 'don't' and 'doesn't' because Spanish uses 'no' for all persons. Remember: 'doesn't' is only for he/she/it.

examples.en: They're married.
examples.es: Están casados.

examples.en: She doesn't work on weekends.
examples.es: Ella no trabaja los fines de semana.

examples.en: My cousins don't work now.
examples.es: Mis primos no trabajan ahora.

commonErrors.why: Use the contraction 'doesn't' (or 'does not'), not 'do not' with he/she/it
'Doesn't' is only for he/she/it; use 'don't' with they

grammar.title: Simple Present Tense - Third Person
grammar.explanation: In English, when we use he, she, or it with simple present verbs, we must add -s or -es to the verb. Unlike Spanish where the verb ending changes for ALL persons (yo trabajo, tú trabajas, él trabaja), English only changes for third person singular. This is a common mistake for Spanish speakers who may forget this -s ending.
grammar.rule: Add -s or -es to the verb when the subject is he, she, it, or a singular noun.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers often forget the -s ending because in Spanish 'él trabaja' sounds different from 'trabajar', but in English 'work' and 'works' sound similar. Remember: he work is WRONG, he works is CORRECT.

examples.en: My sister lives in Miami.
examples.es: Mi hermana vive en Miami.

examples.en: He works at a bank.
examples.es: Él trabaja en un banco.

commonErrors.why: Must add -s to the verb with 'she'

commonErrors.wrong: My brother work at a hospital.
commonErrors.correct: My brother works at a hospital.
commonErrors.why: Singular subjects need -s ending on the verb

grammar.title: Simple Present Questions - Do/Does
grammar.explanation: To make questions in simple present, we use 'do' or 'does' before the subject. Use 'does' with he, she, it, and singular nouns. Use 'do' with I, you, we, they, and plural nouns. IMPORTANT: After 'does', the main verb returns to base form (no -s). Spanish speakers often forget this because Spanish question forms keep the conjugated verb.
grammar.rule: Use 'does' for third person singular (he/she/it) and 'do' for all others; the main verb stays in base form.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers write 'Does she works?' because in Spanish questions keep the conjugated verb ('¿Trabaja ella?'). In English, after 'does', use base form: 'Does she work?' not 'Does she works?'

examples.en: Does your sister live in Miami?
examples.es: ¿Tu hermana vive en Miami?

examples.en: Do your cousins work at the airport?
examples.es: ¿Tus primos trabajan en el aeropuerto?

commonErrors.wrong: Does he works at a bank?
commonErrors.correct: Does he work at a bank?
commonErrors.why: After 'does', use base form of the verb without -s
Use 'does' with third person singular subjects

drillSentences.answer: Does your mom drive to work every day?

grammar.title: Present Continuous for Future Plans
grammar.explanation: English uses present continuous (am/is/are + verb-ing) to talk about future plans or arrangements, especially with life events. This is different from Spanish, which typically uses future tense or 'ir a + infinitive'. For example, 'getting married' = 'casándose' or 'va a casarse'.
grammar.rule: Use present continuous to talk about definite future plans or life events that are happening.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers might say 'He gets married' (present simple) when they mean a future event. In English, use continuous for arranged futures: 'He is getting married' (not 'He gets married').

examples.en: My brother is getting married!
examples.es: ¡Mi hermano se va a casar!

examples.en: My cousin is getting divorced.
examples.es: Mi prima se está divorciando.

commonErrors.correct: She is getting married next month.
commonErrors.why: Use present continuous for definite future plans
Present continuous needs the verb 'to be' (am/is/are)

grammar.title: Responding to News with Social Phrases
grammar.explanation: English has specific phrases to respond to good or bad news. For good news, use 'That's great!', 'Congratulations!', 'Wonderful!'. For bad news, use 'I'm sorry to hear that', 'That's too bad', 'Oh, no'. These are fixed expressions that don't translate word-for-word from Spanish.
grammar.structure: Fixed phrase + (optional follow-up question or comment)
grammar.rule: Use positive phrases for good news and sympathetic phrases for bad news.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers might literally translate '¡Qué bueno!' as 'How good!' which sounds unnatural. Instead, use 'That's great!' or 'Wonderful!'. Similarly, 'Lo siento' means 'I'm sorry' but for news about others, say 'I'm sorry to hear that' (the full phrase).

examples.en: That's great! Congratulations!
examples.es: ¡Qué bien! ¡Felicitaciones!

examples.en: I'm sorry to hear that. Is she OK?
examples.es: Lamento escuchar eso. ¿Ella está bien?

commonErrors.correct: That's great! Your brother is getting married!
commonErrors.why: Use the fixed phrase 'That's great' and present continuous for the event

commonErrors.correct: I'm sorry to hear that. Your cousin is getting divorced.
commonErrors.why: Use the complete phrase 'I'm sorry to hear that' and present continuous

grammar.title: Comparative Adjectives: -er ending
grammar.explanation: En inglés, para comparar dos personas o cosas, añadimos -er al final de adjetivos cortos (1 sílaba). A diferencia del español que usa 'más + adjetivo', el inglés cambia la forma del adjetivo. Siempre usamos 'than' (que) después del adjetivo comparativo.
grammar.rule: For short adjectives (1 syllable), add -er to make the comparative form and use 'than' after it.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian Spanish speakers often say 'more tall' instead of 'taller' because in Spanish we say 'más alto'. In English, we don't use 'more' with short adjectives.

examples.en: I am taller than my brother.
examples.es: Soy más alto que mi hermano.

examples.es: Ella es mayor que yo.

commonErrors.wrong: My father is more old than my mother.
commonErrors.correct: My father is older than my mother.
commonErrors.why: 'Old' is a short adjective, so we add -er, not 'more'.

commonErrors.wrong: I am taller that my sister.
commonErrors.correct: I am taller than my sister.
commonErrors.why: Use 'than' (not 'that') after comparative adjectives.

grammar.title: Comparative Adjectives: more/less + adjective
grammar.explanation: Para adjetivos largos (2+ sílabas) o que terminan en -y, -ful, -ing, -ed, usamos 'more' (más) o 'less' (menos) antes del adjetivo. NO añadimos -er. Esto es similar al español donde decimos 'más interesante' o 'menos aburrido'.
grammar.structure: Subject + verb + more/less + adjective + than + object
grammar.rule: For long adjectives (2+ syllables), use 'more' or 'less' before the adjective, not -er.
grammar.spanishTrap: Students sometimes add -er to long adjectives like 'beautifuler' because they confuse the rules. Remember: long adjectives use 'more/less', short adjectives use -er.

examples.en: This book is more interesting than that one.
examples.es: Este libro es más interesante que ese.

examples.en: She is less athletic than her cousin.
examples.es: Ella es menos atlética que su prima.

commonErrors.wrong: My mom is more hard-workinger than my dad.
commonErrors.correct: My mom is more hard-working than my dad.
commonErrors.why: Long adjectives use 'more', never add -er.

commonErrors.wrong: He is more intelligent that me.
commonErrors.correct: He is more intelligent than me.

grammar.title: Irregular Comparative Adjectives

grammar.rule: Good becomes better, bad becomes worse, and far becomes farther in comparative form.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students often say 'more good' or 'gooder' instead of 'better' because they apply regular rules. These three adjectives are completely irregular and must be memorized.

grammar.title: Intensifying Comparatives with much, a lot, a little
grammar.explanation: Para dar más énfasis a la comparación, usamos 'much' (mucho) o 'a lot' (mucho) antes del comparativo para diferencias grandes, y 'a little' (un poco) para diferencias pequeñas. En español también decimos 'mucho más alto' o 'un poco más alto'.
grammar.structure: Subject + verb + much/a lot/a little + comparative + than + object
grammar.rule: Use 'much', 'a lot', or 'a little' before comparative adjectives to show how big the difference is.
grammar.spanishTrap: Students often forget to use these intensifiers or put them in the wrong position. In English, they always go BEFORE the comparative adjective, just like in Spanish ('mucho más').

grammar.title: Comparative Adjectives with -er and more
grammar.explanation: In English, we use comparative adjectives to compare two people or things. For short adjectives (1 syllable), we add '-er' (tall → taller). For adjectives ending in -y, we change y to i and add -er (funny → funnier). For longer adjectives (2+ syllables), we use 'more' before the adjective (intelligent → more intelligent). Unlike Spanish where you always use 'más', English has two different patterns.
grammar.structure: Subject + verb + adjective-er/more adjective + than + object
grammar.rule: Short adjectives add -er, long adjectives use 'more', and we always use 'than' to introduce the second part of the comparison.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students often say 'more tall' or 'more old' because Spanish uses 'más' for all comparisons (más alto, más viejo). In English, one-syllable adjectives must use -er, not 'more'.

examples.en: My brother is taller than me.
examples.es: Mi hermano es más alto que yo.

examples.en: She is more intelligent than her classmates.
examples.es: Ella es más inteligente que sus compañeros de clase.

commonErrors.wrong: He is more tall than his sister.

commonErrors.why: One-syllable adjectives like 'tall' use -er, not 'more'.

commonErrors.wrong: My car is faster that yours.
commonErrors.correct: My car is faster than yours.
commonErrors.why: We use 'than' (not 'that') to introduce the second part of a comparison.

grammar.title: Intensifying Comparatives with 'much' and 'a lot'
grammar.explanation: To make comparisons stronger, we use 'much' or 'a lot' before the comparative adjective. This is similar to Spanish 'mucho más'. We say 'much funnier' or 'a lot taller', never 'very funnier'. Unlike Spanish where you can say 'muy más', English doesn't use 'very' with comparatives.
grammar.structure: Subject + verb + much/a lot + comparative adjective + than + object
grammar.rule: Use 'much' or 'a lot' (not 'very') to intensify comparative adjectives.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students often say 'very more tall' because in Spanish you can use 'muy' or 'mucho' interchangeably. In English, only 'much' or 'a lot' work with comparatives, never 'very'.

examples.en: He is much funnier than I am.
examples.es: Él es mucho más gracioso que yo.

examples.en: This exercise is a lot easier than the last one.

commonErrors.wrong: My sister is very taller than me.

commonErrors.why: We use 'much' or 'a lot', not 'very', to intensify comparatives.

grammar.title: Irregular Comparative Adjectives
grammar.explanation: Some common adjectives have irregular comparative forms that don't follow the -er or more pattern. The most important ones are: good → better (not 'gooder'), bad → worse (not 'badder'), far → farther/further. These must be memorized because they change completely. Spanish also has irregulars (bueno → mejor), but they don't match English exactly.
grammar.structure: Subject + verb + irregular comparative + than + object
grammar.rule: Memorize irregular comparatives: good → better, bad → worse, far → farther/further.
grammar.spanishTrap: Students often say 'more good' or 'more bad' because they try to apply the regular pattern. These adjectives have completely irregular forms in English, just like in Spanish (mejor, peor).

examples.en: This restaurant is better than the other one.

commonErrors.why: 'Bad' becomes 'worse' in comparative form, not 'more bad'.

grammar.title: Using 'even though' to show contrast
grammar.explanation: We use 'even though' to introduce a surprising contrast between two ideas. It means 'although' or 'despite the fact that'. In Spanish, this is similar to 'aunque' or 'a pesar de que'. 'Even though' is always followed by a subject and verb, creating a complete clause. It emphasizes that something is surprising or unexpected.
grammar.structure: Even though + subject + verb, main clause OR Main clause + even though + subject + verb
grammar.rule: 'Even though' introduces a contrast clause and must be followed by a subject and verb.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students sometimes confuse 'even though' with 'even if' or forget to include both subject and verb after it. Remember: 'even though' = aunque (for facts), 'even if' = aunque (for hypothetical situations).

examples.en: Even though I'm the older sibling, he's taller than me.
examples.es: Aunque soy el hermano mayor, él es más alto que yo.

examples.en: She passed the exam even though she didn't study much.

commonErrors.wrong: Even though tired, I went to the party.
commonErrors.correct: Even though I was tired, I went to the party.
commonErrors.why: 'Even though' must be followed by a subject and verb, not just an adjective.

commonErrors.wrong: Even I'm hungry, I won't eat now.
commonErrors.correct: Even though I'm hungry, I won't eat now.
commonErrors.why: To show contrast, use 'even though', not just 'even'.

grammar.title: Using 'Both' and 'Neither' to compare
grammar.explanation: Use 'both' to say two people or things share something. Use 'neither' to say two people or things do NOT share something. Unlike Spanish 'ninguno', 'neither' takes a positive verb form in English. 'Both' is always followed by a plural noun or 'of + pronoun/article'.
grammar.structure: Both + plural noun / Both of + pronoun | Neither + singular noun / Neither of + pronoun + singular verb
grammar.rule: 'Both' refers to two things together (positive); 'neither' refers to two things together (negative) with positive verb form.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian Spanish speakers often use double negatives ('ninguno no come') but English says 'neither eats' (positive verb form after neither).

grammar.title: Comparative adjectives with 'than'
grammar.explanation: To compare two people or things, add '-er' to short adjectives (tall → taller) or use 'more' before long adjectives (athletic → more athletic). Always use 'than' after the comparative form. Unlike Spanish 'más... que', English requires only one word 'than'.
grammar.structure: Subject + verb + comparative adjective + than + noun/pronoun
grammar.rule: Short adjectives (1-2 syllables) add '-er'; long adjectives (3+ syllables) use 'more'.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers often forget 'than' or use 'that' instead. Spanish says 'más alto que' but English needs 'taller than' (not 'taller that').

examples.en: Jonah is taller than Brandon.
examples.es: Jonah es más alto que Brandon.

commonErrors.wrong: My brother is more tall than me.

grammar.title: Adjectives ending in '-ly': 'likely' usage
grammar.explanation: Some adjectives end in '-ly' (likely, friendly, lovely). These are adjectives, not adverbs. Use 'more likely' for comparisons, not 'likelier'. In Spanish, these translate differently: 'likely' = 'probable', 'friendly' = 'amigable'.
grammar.structure: Subject + verb + more likely + to + base verb
grammar.rule: Use 'more likely' (not 'likelier') to compare probability; 'likely' is followed by 'to + verb'.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish uses 'es probable que + subjunctive' but English uses 'is likely to + infinitive' (no subjunctive).

examples.en: Identical twins are more likely to look alike.
examples.es: Los gemelos idénticos son más propensos a parecerse.

grammar.title: Describing similarities with 'look alike' and 'dress alike'
grammar.explanation: The phrase 'look alike' means two people appear similar. 'Dress alike' means they wear similar clothes. These are two-word verbs. Unlike Spanish 'parecerse' (reflexive), English 'look alike' has no reflexive form.
grammar.rule: 'Alike' comes after the verb 'look' or 'dress' to show similarity between two or more people.

grammar.title: Linking sounds with 'does she/he'
grammar.explanation: In natural English speech, when a word ends in a consonant and the next word begins with a vowel, we connect them smoothly. This is called linking. 'Does she' sounds like /dʌz-ʃi/ and 'does he' sounds like /dʌz-i/. Unlike Spanish where each syllable is pronounced separately, English flows words together.
grammar.rule: Connect the final 's' sound of 'does' with the vowel sound that follows in 'she/he'.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers often pause between words and pronounce each syllable separately. In English, you must connect sounds smoothly for natural pronunciation.

examples.en: Does she have any cousins?
examples.es: ¿Ella tiene primos?

examples.en: Where does he live?

commonErrors.why: After 'does', use the base verb without 's'
The 's' is already in 'does', so the verb stays in base form

grammar.title: Describing similarities with 'both'
grammar.explanation: We use 'both' to talk about two people or things together when they share the same characteristic. 'Both' goes before the verb or after 'be'. In Spanish you might say 'los dos' or 'ambos', but the word order in English is different. Example: 'They both love music' NOT 'Both they love music'.
grammar.structure: Subject + both + verb / Both + subject + verb + complement
grammar.rule: 'Both' comes after the subject and before the main verb, or at the beginning with emphasis.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers often put 'ambos/both' in the wrong position. Remember: 'They both work' NOT 'Both they work' in standard sentences.

examples.en: They both love action movies.
examples.es: A ambos les encantan las películas de acción.

examples.en: Both my parents are engineers.
examples.es: Ambos mis padres son ingenieros.

commonErrors.why: 'Both' comes after the subject in simple sentences
Use plural verb 'are' with plural subject

drillSentences.prompt: Mis abuelos tienen ochenta años.
drillSentences.answer: My grandparents are both eighty years old.

drillSentences.prompt: My two best friends speak French. They ___ studied in Paris last year.
drillSentences.answer: both

drillSentences.prompt: Both my dogs is very friendly with children.
drillSentences.answer: Both my dogs are very friendly with children.
drillSentences.hint: Use plural verb with plural subject

grammar.title: Possessive 's for family relationships
grammar.explanation: To show that someone belongs to or is related to another person, we add 's after the person's name or noun. This is the possessive form. Unlike Spanish where you use 'de' (el hermano de Juan), English puts the 's directly on the owner: 'Juan's brother'. Be careful: it's 'my sister's husband' NOT 'the husband of my sister' in natural English.
grammar.rule: Add 's to show possession or relationship.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish uses 'de' in reverse order (el esposo de mi hermana), but English uses 's and puts the possessor first: 'my sister's husband'. Don't translate word-by-word from Spanish.

examples.en: My brother's wife is a teacher.
examples.es: La esposa de mi hermano es profesora.

examples.en: Paula's personality is very friendly.
examples.es: La personalidad de Paula es muy amigable.

commonErrors.wrong: The car of my father is new.
commonErrors.why: Use possessive 's, not 'of' for people
You must include the apostrophe before s for possessive

drillSentences.prompt: El computador de mi primo es muy rápido.

grammar.title: Present Simple for Facts and General Truths
grammar.explanation: We use the present simple to talk about facts, general truths, and habitual actions. Unlike Spanish where you can say 'vive' or 'está viviendo', English clearly separates simple facts (lives) from ongoing actions (is living). For facts about families and statistics, always use present simple.
grammar.rule: Add -s or -es to the verb when the subject is he, she, it, or a singular noun.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian speakers often forget the -s ending for third person singular (he/she/it). In Spanish, 'vive' works for all subjects, but in English you must say 'he lives' not 'he live'.

examples.en: Many adult children live with their parents.
examples.es: Muchos hijos adultos viven con sus padres.

examples.en: A traditional household consists of two parents.
examples.es: Un hogar tradicional consiste de dos padres.

commonErrors.why: Third person singular (she) needs -s ending

commonErrors.wrong: My brother help with the chores.
commonErrors.correct: My brother helps with the chores.
commonErrors.why: Singular subject (brother) requires verb + s

drillSentences.prompt: Mi profesor enseña matemáticas en la universidad.

grammar.title: Prepositions with Age and Time
grammar.explanation: In English, we say someone is 'at least 18 years old' or 'until they are 30'. Unlike Spanish where you use 'tener' (to have) for age, English uses 'to be'. Also, 'until' marks the end point of an action, similar to 'hasta' in Spanish.
grammar.rule: Use 'at least' to show minimum age or amount, and 'until' to show when something stops.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian speakers often translate directly from 'tener años' and say 'have years' instead of 'be years old'. Also, they may confuse 'until' with 'to' when translating 'hasta'.

examples.en: They live at home until they are at least 20.
examples.es: Ellos viven en casa hasta que tienen al menos 20 años.

examples.en: She stayed with her parents until she was 25.
examples.es: Ella se quedó con sus padres hasta que tenía 25 años.

commonErrors.why: Use 'be' not 'have' for age in English

commonErrors.wrong: I study to 5 p.m. every day.
commonErrors.correct: I study until 5 p.m. every day.
commonErrors.why: Use 'until' to show when an action stops

grammar.title: Quantifiers: Fractions and Percentages
grammar.explanation: We use fractions (one-third, two-thirds) and percentages (70%, 90%) to describe quantities. Unlike Spanish where you might say 'la tercera parte', English has specific fraction words. When using these with 'of', the verb agrees with the noun after 'of', not the fraction.
grammar.rule: The verb agrees with the noun after 'of': 'Two-thirds of children live...' (plural) but 'Two-thirds of the family lives...' (singular).
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian speakers may struggle with fraction vocabulary and try to translate literally ('two of three' instead of 'two-thirds'). Also, they may make the verb agree with the fraction instead of the following noun.

examples.en: About 70% of all households are multi-generational.
examples.es: Aproximadamente el 70% de todos los hogares son multigeneracionales.

examples.en: One-third of all children live with a single parent.
examples.es: Un tercio de todos los niños viven con un padre soltero.

commonErrors.wrong: Two-thirds of students is from Colombia.
commonErrors.correct: Two-thirds of students are from Colombia.
commonErrors.why: Verb agrees with 'students' (plural), not 'two-thirds'

commonErrors.wrong: About 20 percent of the class speak English.
commonErrors.correct: About 20 percent of the class speaks English.
commonErrors.why: Verb agrees with 'class' (singular), not 'percent'

grammar.title: Vocabulary: Family Relationship Terms
grammar.explanation: English has specific compound words for family relationships: ex-husband (former husband), grandchildren (children of your children), multi-generational (many generations together). Unlike Spanish where you often use 'de' phrases ('hijos de mis hijos'), English combines words into one term.
grammar.rule: Use hyphens for 'ex-' relationships and combine 'grand-' directly with the family word.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian speakers may translate literally ('the husband before' instead of 'ex-husband') or separate compound words ('grand mother' instead of 'grandmother'). Also, 'parents' means mother AND father, not relatives in general like 'parientes'.

examples.en: Her ex-husband visits the grandchildren every Sunday.
examples.es: Su exesposo visita a los nietos cada domingo.

examples.en: We live in a multi-generational household with three generations.
examples.es: Vivimos en un hogar multigeneracional con tres generaciones.

commonErrors.wrong: My before wife lives in another city.
commonErrors.correct: My ex-wife lives in another city.
commonErrors.why: Use 'ex-' prefix for former spouse

commonErrors.wrong: My grand mother is 75 years old.
commonErrors.why: Write 'grandmother' as one word, no space

grammar.title: Present Simple for General Facts and Habits
grammar.explanation: We use the present simple to talk about general facts, habits, and situations that are generally true. Unlike Spanish, where you might use present continuous for habits, English uses simple present. Add -s/-es to verbs with he/she/it.
grammar.structure: Subject + base verb (+ s/es for he/she/it) + complement
grammar.rule: Use present simple for facts, routines, and permanent situations.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian students often say 'She is living with her parents' (presente continuo) when they mean a permanent situation. In English, use 'She lives with her parents' for permanent situations.

examples.en: Many young adults leave home when they get married.
examples.es: Muchos adultos jóvenes se van de casa cuando se casan.

examples.en: Single-parent households are very common in North America.
examples.es: Los hogares monoparentales son muy comunes en Norteamérica.

commonErrors.why: Add -s to the verb with he/she/it subjects
Use 'don't' (not doesn't) with plural subjects

drillSentences.answer: My sister studies medicine at university.

drillSentences.answer: eats

grammar.title: Question Formation with Do/Does
grammar.explanation: To make questions in present simple, we use do/does + subject + base verb. Use 'does' with he/she/it and 'do' with I/you/we/they. Unlike Spanish, we cannot just use question intonation - we must use the auxiliary verb.
grammar.rule: Always use the auxiliary do/does at the beginning of yes/no questions in present simple.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers often forget the auxiliary and say 'You know anyone?' instead of 'Do you know anyone?' In English, the auxiliary is required for questions.

examples.en: Do you know anyone who lives in a multi-generational household?
examples.es: ¿Conoces a alguien que viva en un hogar multigeneracional?

examples.en: Does your country have many single-parent families?
examples.es: ¿Tu país tiene muchas familias monoparentales?

commonErrors.why: After does/do, use the base verb without -s
Questions require the auxiliary do/does

drillSentences.prompt: ¿Tu hermano tiene carro?
drillSentences.answer: Does your brother have a car?

drillSentences.prompt: ___ your parents work on weekends? They seem very busy.
drillSentences.answer: Do

drillSentences.prompt: Does Maria speaks English well?
drillSentences.answer: Does Maria speak English well?

grammar.title: Comparatives and Superlatives
grammar.explanation: We use comparative adjectives to compare two things (more common, bigger) and superlatives for three or more (most common, biggest). Short adjectives add -er/-est, while longer adjectives use more/most. Unlike Spanish, where you always use 'más', English changes the adjective form.
grammar.structure: Comparative: adjective + -er + than OR more + adjective + than; Superlative: the + adjective + -est OR the most + adjective
grammar.rule: One-syllable adjectives use -er/-est; adjectives with 3+ syllables use more/most.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers often say 'more big' instead of 'bigger' or 'more common' for two-syllable words. Remember: short adjectives change form, they don't use 'more'.

examples.en: Multi-generational households are more common in Asia than in Europe.
examples.es: Los hogares multigeneracionales son más comunes en Asia que en Europa.

examples.en: This is the biggest change in family trends.
examples.es: Este es el cambio más grande en las tendencias familiares.

commonErrors.wrong: She is more tall than her brother.
commonErrors.correct: She is taller than her brother.
commonErrors.why: Short adjectives use -er, not 'more'

commonErrors.wrong: This is the most big house.
commonErrors.why: Short adjectives use -est, not 'most'

drillSentences.prompt: Mi teléfono es más caro que el tuyo.
drillSentences.answer: My phone is more expensive than yours.

drillSentences.prompt: Math is the ___ difficult subject for me. I always fail the tests.
drillSentences.answer: most

drillSentences.prompt: Colombia is more hot than Canada.
drillSentences.answer: Colombia is hotter than Canada.

grammar.title: When Clauses for Time Relationships
grammar.explanation: We use 'when' to connect two actions or situations, showing a time relationship. Both clauses usually use the same tense when talking about general habits or facts. Unlike Spanish 'cuando', English 'when' doesn't change verb mood.
grammar.structure: Main clause + when + time clause OR When + time clause, main clause
grammar.rule: Use 'when' to show time relationships between two actions or situations.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish uses subjunctive after 'cuando' for future events (cuando tenga tiempo), but English uses present simple with 'when' even for future meaning (when I have time).

examples.en: Children usually leave home when they get a job.
examples.es: Los niños usualmente se van de casa cuando consiguen un trabajo.

examples.en: When young people get married, they often move to a new house.
examples.es: Cuando los jóvenes se casan, a menudo se mudan a una casa nueva.

commonErrors.wrong: When I will finish school, I will travel.
commonErrors.correct: When I finish school, I will travel.
commonErrors.why: Use present simple (not future) in the when-clause for future events

commonErrors.wrong: I call you when I will arrive.
commonErrors.correct: I call you when I arrive.
commonErrors.why: No future tense after when in time clauses

drillSentences.prompt: Cuando llueve, no puedo jugar fútbol afuera.
drillSentences.answer: When it rains, I can't play soccer outside.

drillSentences.prompt: My mom always cooks arepa ___ we visit on Sundays. It's our family tradition.

exercises.question: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Does children usually leave home at 18?
Do children usually leave home at 18?
Do children usually leaves home at 18?
Does children usually leaves home at 18?

exercises.explanation: Use 'do' with plural subjects and the base verb form.

grammar.title: Want + infinitive (to express purpose)
grammar.explanation: En inglés, usamos 'want to' + verbo infinitivo para expresar deseos o intenciones. A diferencia del español donde puedes decir 'Quiero conocer' sin preposición antes del verbo infinitivo, en inglés SIEMPRE necesitas 'to' entre 'want' y el verbo principal.
grammar.rule: Use 'want to' + base verb to express desires or intentions; 'to' is always required before the infinitive verb.
grammar.spanishTrap: Los hispanohablantes olvidan la preposición 'to' porque en español 'quiero' va directamente seguido del infinitivo sin preposición.

grammar.title: Prepositions with nouns (in, from, with)
grammar.explanation: Las preposiciones 'in', 'from' y 'with' tienen usos específicos en inglés. 'In' se usa para lugares o situaciones (in my work, in another country), 'from' indica origen (from a lot of countries), y 'with' indica compañía o instrumento (with people). No siempre corresponden directamente con las preposiciones españolas.
grammar.rule: Use 'in' for location/context, 'from' for origin, and 'with' for accompaniment or instrument.
grammar.spanishTrap: Los hispanohablantes confunden 'in' y 'on' porque ambos pueden traducirse como 'en' en español.

grammar.title: Present continuous for ongoing reasons (be + verb-ing)
grammar.explanation: En inglés, usamos el presente continuo (be + gerundio) para hablar de acciones en progreso o situaciones actuales. A diferencia del español, donde decimos 'estudio inglés para trabajar', en inglés usamos 'I am studying English for work'. Se forma con el verbo 'to be' (am/is/are) + verbo con -ing.
grammar.rule: Use 'be + verb-ing' to talk about current learning activities and their purposes
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian Spanish speakers often drop the auxiliary 'be' and say 'I studying' instead of 'I am studying'

grammar.title: It + be + adjective + (to + verb / for + noun)
grammar.explanation: En inglés, usamos 'It' como sujeto impersonal seguido de 'is' + adjetivo para expresar características generales. A diferencia del español, donde decimos 'Es útil para comunicarse', en inglés siempre necesitamos el pronombre 'It': 'It is useful for communicating'. Esta estructura es muy común para describir cualidades del inglés.
grammar.structure: It + is + adjective + (to + base verb / for + gerund/noun)
grammar.rule: Use 'It is + adjective' to describe general characteristics or qualities
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers often omit 'It' because in Spanish we say 'Es útil' not 'Ello es útil'. English requires the subject pronoun 'It'

grammar.title: Questions with 'Why' and 'How many'
grammar.explanation: En inglés, usamos 'Why' para preguntar por razones y 'How many' para preguntar por cantidades. A diferencia del español, el orden es: palabra interrogativa + verbo auxiliar + sujeto + verbo principal. Por ejemplo: 'Why study English?' o 'How many students are studying?'. El verbo auxiliar es necesario en preguntas completas.
grammar.structure: Why + (auxiliary) + subject + verb...? / How many + noun + auxiliary + subject + verb...?
grammar.rule: Use 'Why' to ask for reasons and 'How many' to ask about quantities with countable nouns
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers often forget the auxiliary verb in questions, saying 'Why you study?' instead of 'Why do you study?' or keep Spanish word order

grammar.explanation: En inglés, usamos 'let me introduce you' para presentar a alguien. A diferencia del español donde decimos 'te presento a...', en inglés usamos 'let me' (déjame) seguido de 'introduce you to' y el nombre de la persona. Esta estructura es formal y cortés.
grammar.structure: Let me + introduce + you/you all + to + person
grammar.rule: Use 'let me introduce you to' to formally present someone to another person or group
grammar.spanishTrap: En español decimos 'te presento a' directamente, pero en inglés debemos usar 'let me introduce you to' (no 'I present you to').

examples.en: Let me introduce you all to my wife, Sunny.
examples.es: Déjame presentarles a todos a mi esposa, Sunny.

examples.en: Nice to meet you, Mr. and Mrs. Jin-soo Park.
examples.es: Mucho gusto, Sr. y Sra. Jin-soo Park.

commonErrors.wrong: I present you to my wife.
commonErrors.correct: Let me introduce you to my wife.
commonErrors.why: We don't translate 'te presento' literally; use 'let me introduce' instead

commonErrors.wrong: Let me introduce to you my wife.
commonErrors.correct: Let me introduce you to my wife.
commonErrors.why: The word order is 'introduce you to', not 'introduce to you'

grammar.title: Polite greetings: 'It's a pleasure to meet you'
grammar.explanation: En inglés formal, usamos 'It's a pleasure to meet you' (es un placer conocerte) cuando conocemos a alguien. A diferencia del español donde decimos 'mucho gusto' como una frase fija, en inglés usamos una oración completa con 'it's a pleasure'. También podemos responder 'too' (también) al final.
grammar.structure: It's a pleasure to + meet + you (+ too)
grammar.rule: Use 'It's a pleasure to meet you' as a formal way to greet someone when you first meet
grammar.spanishTrap: No traducir 'mucho gusto' literalmente como 'much pleasure'. En inglés se dice 'It's a pleasure to meet you'.

examples.en: It's a pleasure to meet you, too.
examples.es: Es un placer conocerte también.

examples.en: Nice to meet you, Mr. and Mrs. Jin-soo Park.
examples.es: Mucho gusto, Sr. y Sra. Jin-soo Park.

commonErrors.correct: It's a pleasure to meet you.
commonErrors.why: Don't translate 'mucho gusto' literally; use the complete English phrase

commonErrors.correct: It's a pleasure to meet you.
commonErrors.why: You need 'It' at the beginning and 'to' before 'meet'

grammar.title: Questions with 'Are you...?' and 'Do you...?'
grammar.explanation: En inglés, para hacer preguntas usamos 'are you' con el verbo 'to be' (¿eres tú...?) y 'do you' con otros verbos (¿hablas...?). A diferencia del español donde solo cambiamos la entonación, en inglés debemos cambiar el orden de las palabras y usar el auxiliar 'do' con verbos principales.
grammar.structure: Are you + noun/adjective? / Do you + verb?
grammar.rule: Use 'are you' for identity/state questions and 'do you' for action questions
grammar.spanishTrap: En español preguntamos '¿Hablas inglés?' sin auxiliar, pero en inglés necesitamos 'Do you speak English?', no 'You speak English?'

examples.en: Are you on the nine o'clock tour?
examples.es: ¿Estás en el tour de las nueve?

examples.en: Does everyone here speak English?
examples.es: ¿Todos aquí hablan inglés?

commonErrors.why: In English questions with action verbs, we must use 'do' or 'does'
'Are' is only for 'be'; use 'do' with other verbs like 'speak'

grammar.title: Present simple: 'where are you from?' vs 'I'm from...'
grammar.explanation: Para preguntar y responder sobre origen, en inglés usamos 'where are you from?' (¿de dónde eres?) y 'I'm from + lugar' (soy de...). Igual que en español, usamos el verbo 'to be' (ser/estar), pero en inglés siempre necesitamos el pronombre 'I' antes del verbo.
grammar.structure: Where are you from? / I'm from + place / We're from + place
grammar.rule: Use 'where are you from' to ask about origin and 'I'm from' plus a place to answer
grammar.spanishTrap: En español podemos omitir el pronombre ('Soy de Ecuador'), pero en inglés SIEMPRE necesitamos el pronombre: 'I'm from Ecuador', no 'Am from Ecuador'.

examples.en: Well, I'm originally from Ecuador, but Marty's from the States.
examples.es: Bueno, soy originaria de Ecuador, pero Marty es de los Estados.

examples.en: We're from Seoul, South Korea.
examples.es: Somos de Seúl, Corea del Sur.

commonErrors.why: In English, you must always include the subject pronoun 'I'
The word order is 'originally from', not 'from originally'

grammar.title: Starting conversations: 'Excuse me'
grammar.explanation: En inglés, 'Excuse me' se usa para iniciar una conversación cortésmente con alguien que no conoces, similar a 'disculpe' o 'perdón' en español. A diferencia del español donde podemos omitirlo, en inglés es muy importante usarlo para ser cortés, especialmente con desconocidos.
grammar.structure: Excuse me. + your question or statement
grammar.rule: Use 'Excuse me' at the beginning to politely start a conversation with people you don't know
grammar.spanishTrap: No confundir 'excuse me' (para iniciar conversación) con 'sorry' (para disculparse). 'Excuse me' se usa ANTES de hablar, 'sorry' DESPUÉS de un error.

examples.en: Excuse me. Are you on the nine o'clock tour?
examples.es: Disculpe. ¿Estás en el tour de las nueve?

examples.en: Excuse me. Nice to meet you.
examples.es: Disculpe. Mucho gusto.

commonErrors.wrong: Sorry, are you on the tour?
commonErrors.correct: Excuse me, are you on the tour?
commonErrors.why: 'Sorry' is for apologizing; use 'excuse me' to start a conversation

commonErrors.correct: Excuse me. Are you from Seoul?
commonErrors.why: The complete phrase is 'excuse me', not just 'excuse'

grammar.title: Information questions with be
grammar.explanation: En inglés, las preguntas de información comienzan con palabras interrogativas (What, Who, Where, When, How) seguidas del verbo be. A diferencia del español, donde el verbo puede ir después del sujeto, en inglés el verbo be siempre va inmediatamente después de la palabra interrogativa. El orden es: Wh-word + be + subject.
grammar.rule: Information questions begin with What, Who, Where, When, or How, followed by the verb be.
grammar.spanishTrap: En español se puede decir '¿Quién tu profesor es?' pero en inglés el verbo be SIEMPRE va después de la palabra interrogativa: 'Who is your teacher?' El orden sujeto-verbo del español no funciona aquí.

'From' goes at the end when asking about origin

grammar.title: Contractions with be
grammar.explanation: Las contracciones combinan un pronombre o nombre con el verbo be usando un apóstrofo. En español no existe este concepto. 'What is' se convierte en 'What's', 'Where is' en 'Where's', 'it is' en 'it's', etc. Se usan en inglés hablado y escrito informal.
grammar.rule: Contractions combine pronouns or question words with be using an apostrophe: What's = What is, he's = he is, she's = she is, it's = it is, you're = you are, we're = we are, they're = they are.
grammar.spanishTrap: Los hispanohablantes confunden 'it's' (it is) con 'its' (su, posesivo). 'It's' SIEMPRE significa 'it is' o 'it has', nunca es posesivo.

examples.en: What's = What is

examples.en: Where's = Where is

examples.es: él es / él está

examples.en: she's = she is

examples.en: it's = it is

examples.en: you're = you are

examples.en: we're = we are
examples.es: nosotros somos

examples.en: they're = they are
examples.es: ellos son / ellas son

commonErrors.why: 'It's' (with apostrophe) means 'it is'. 'Its' (no apostrophe) is possessive
In spoken and informal English, we typically use contractions

grammar.title: Possessive nouns and adjectives
grammar.explanation: Para mostrar posesión de una persona singular, agregamos 's (apóstrofo + s) al final del nombre. En español se usa 'de' pero en inglés se usa el apóstrofo: 'el email de George' = 'George's email'. También usamos adjetivos posesivos como 'your', 'her', 'my'.
grammar.rule: Add 's to a person's name to show possession. Use possessive adjectives (my, your, his, her, its, our, their) before nouns.
grammar.spanishTrap: En español se dice 'el profesor de María' (de + persona) pero en inglés es 'Maria's teacher' (persona + 's). El orden es opuesto y no se usa 'de' o 'of'.

grammar.title: Contractions of the verb be
grammar.explanation: En inglés, es muy común contraer (acortar) el verbo 'be' en conversaciones. A diferencia del español donde siempre escribimos 'yo soy', en inglés se prefiere decir 'I'm' en lugar de 'I am'. Estas contracciones son más naturales en conversación.
grammar.rule: Use contractions of be (I'm, he's, she's, it's, you're, we're, they're) when possible in conversation.
grammar.spanishTrap: Los hispanohablantes a menudo olvidan usar contracciones porque en español no existen de esta manera. Debes recordar que 'I'm' es más natural que 'I am' en conversación.

grammar.title: Using 'Same here' to express agreement

grammar.rule: Use 'Same here' to show you have the same opinion when you agree with someone.

grammar.title: Yes/No questions with 'be' and short answers
grammar.explanation: En inglés, para hacer preguntas con el verbo 'be', invertimos el orden: el verbo va antes del sujeto. A diferencia del español (donde decimos '¿Eres casado?'), en inglés decimos 'Are you married?'. Las respuestas cortas usan 'Yes' o 'No' + pronombre + verbo 'be', nunca repetimos el adjetivo.
grammar.structure: Are/Is + subject + adjective/noun? → Yes, subject + am/is/are. / No, subject + am not/isn't/aren't.
grammar.rule: To make yes/no questions with 'be', put the verb before the subject. Answer with yes/no + subject pronoun + be verb.
grammar.spanishTrap: En español decimos 'Sí' o 'No' solo, pero en inglés debemos agregar el pronombre y el verbo: 'Yes, I am' no solo 'Yes'. También, los colombianos a veces olvidan la contracción negativa: decimos 'No, I'm not' o 'No, they aren't', nunca 'No, I amn't'.

examples.en: Are you married? Yes, I am.
examples.es: ¿Estás casado? Sí, lo estoy.

examples.en: Is she Chinese? No, she's not.
examples.es: ¿Es ella china? No, no lo es.

commonErrors.correct: Are you married? Yes, I am.
commonErrors.why: Short answers need the subject pronoun and verb 'be', not just 'yes' or 'no'

commonErrors.wrong: Is your birthplace Sao Paulo? Yes, it's.
commonErrors.correct: Is your birthplace Sao Paulo? Yes, it is.
commonErrors.why: In affirmative short answers, we don't use contractions with 'is'

grammar.title: Contractions with 'be' in questions and negatives
grammar.explanation: En inglés usamos contracciones (formas cortas) con 'be' en preguntas negativas y en respuestas negativas. Ejemplos: 'isn't' = is not, 'aren't' = are not. A diferencia del español, estas contracciones son muy comunes en inglés hablado. IMPORTANTE: En respuestas cortas afirmativas NO usamos contracciones con 'is', 'are': decimos 'Yes, she is' (NO 'Yes, she's').
grammar.structure: Question: Isn't/Aren't + subject...? / Negative answer: No, subject + 'm not/isn't/aren't

grammar.title: Yes/No Questions vs Information Questions - Intonation
grammar.explanation: En inglés, la entonación cambia según el tipo de pregunta. Las preguntas de sí/no (yes/no questions) usan entonación ascendente ↗, como cuando preguntas algo en español con tono de duda. Las preguntas de información (con what, where, who, etc.) usan entonación descendente ↘, como cuando haces una pregunta directa en español.
grammar.rule: Use rising intonation in yes/no questions. Use falling intonation in information questions.
grammar.spanishTrap: Los colombianos tienden a usar entonación ascendente en todas las preguntas, pero en inglés las preguntas con what, where, who, etc. requieren entonación descendente.

examples.en: Is she single? ↗
examples.es: ¿Es ella soltera? ↗

examples.en: Are they from Canada? ↗
examples.es: ¿Son ellos de Canadá? ↗

examples.en: What's her marital status? ↘
examples.es: ¿Cuál es su estado civil? ↘

examples.en: Where are they from? ↘
examples.es: ¿De dónde son ellos? ↘

commonErrors.why: Information questions need falling intonation, not rising
Yes/no questions need rising intonation

grammar.title: Information Questions with be (What, Where)
grammar.explanation: Para hacer preguntas de información con el verbo 'be', se usa la estructura: palabra interrogativa (what, where) + verbo be + sujeto. A diferencia del español donde dices '¿Cuál es...?' o '¿Dónde están...?', en inglés el verbo be va ANTES del sujeto.
grammar.rule: In information questions with be, the question word comes first, then the verb be, then the subject.
grammar.spanishTrap: Los colombianos a menudo dicen 'What is your marital status?' correctamente, pero pueden confundirse con el orden en preguntas más largas. Recuerda: la palabra interrogativa siempre va primero, luego el verbo.

examples.es: ¿Cuál es su estado civil?

examples.en: Where are they from?

examples.en: What's your nationality?

commonErrors.why: The verb 'is' must come before the subject in questions
Use 'what' for asking which language, not 'where'

grammar.title: Yes/No Questions with be
grammar.explanation: Para hacer preguntas de sí/no con el verbo 'be', se invierte el orden: el verbo be va ANTES del sujeto. En español dices '¿Eres tú...?' o '¿Está ella...?', y en inglés es similar: el verbo va primero. La respuesta corta es 'Yes, [subject] + be' o 'No, [subject] + be + not'.
grammar.rule: In yes/no questions with be, put the verb be before the subject.
grammar.spanishTrap: En español, puedes decir '¿Tú eres de Canadá?' o '¿Eres de Canadá?'. En inglés, el verbo SIEMPRE va primero en preguntas: 'Are you from Canada?', nunca 'You are from Canada?'.

grammar.title: Responding with Interest - Social Language
grammar.explanation: En conversaciones en inglés, es importante mostrar interés cuando alguien te cuenta algo. Se usan expresiones cortas como 'Interesting!', 'Wow!', 'Really?', 'No way!' y 'That's great!'. Es como decir en español '¡Qué interesante!', '¡Guau!', '¿De verdad?', '¡No puede ser!' o '¡Qué bien!'.
grammar.rule: Use short expressions like 'Interesting!', 'Wow!', 'Really?', 'No way!', 'That's great!' to show interest in conversation.
grammar.spanishTrap: Los colombianos pueden traducir literalmente '¡Qué interesante!' como 'How interesting!' pero en inglés casual se dice simplemente 'Interesting!'.

grammar.title: Introductions - Meeting Someone
grammar.explanation: Para presentarte en inglés, usas expresiones como 'Are you [name]?', 'Yes, I am', 'It's great to meet you', 'I'm [name]' y '[Name] for short'. Es similar al español pero con estructuras fijas. 'For short' significa 'para abreviar' y se usa con apodos.

grammar.rule: When introducing yourself, state your name clearly and respond positively when meeting someone.
grammar.spanishTrap: En español dices 'Mucho gusto', pero en inglés se dice 'It's great to meet you' o 'Good to meet you', no 'Much pleasure'.

grammar.title: Career vs. Occupation: Distinguishing Future Goals and Current Work
grammar.explanation: En inglés, 'career' se refiere a tus planes profesionales a largo plazo (lo que estudias o quieres ser), mientras que 'occupation' es tu trabajo actual. La página enseña: 'I'm studying for a career in architecture, but I'm working as a restaurant manager right now. That's my current occupation.' En español, ambos pueden traducirse como 'carrera' o 'trabajo', pero en inglés la distinción es clara.
grammar.structure: I'm studying for a career in [field] / That's my current occupation
grammar.rule: Use 'career' for the profession you are preparing for or planning; use 'occupation' for the job you are doing now.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian Spanish speakers often use 'carrera' for both concepts. Remember: 'career' = future/long-term goal; 'occupation' = what you do right now for work.

examples.en: I'm studying for a career in architecture, but I'm working as a restaurant manager right now.
examples.es: Estoy estudiando para una carrera en arquitectura, pero estoy trabajando como gerente de restaurante ahora mismo.

examples.en: That's my current occupation.
examples.es: Esa es mi ocupación actual.

commonErrors.wrong: I'm studying for an occupation in medicine.
commonErrors.correct: I'm studying for a career in medicine.
commonErrors.why: Use 'career' for future professional goals, not 'occupation'.

commonErrors.wrong: My career right now is manager.
commonErrors.why: 'Occupation' describes your current job, not 'career'.

grammar.title: Gerunds after 'enjoy' and Prepositions
grammar.explanation: Después de verbos como 'enjoy' y después de preposiciones como 'good with', usamos el gerundio (-ing). La página muestra: 'Miranda enjoys talking to people' y 'I'm really good with computers.' A diferencia del español, donde usamos el infinitivo ('disfrutar hablar'), en inglés siempre usamos la forma -ing después de 'enjoy'.
grammar.rule: After 'enjoy', always use the gerund form (verb + -ing). After 'good with', use a noun or noun phrase.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish uses the infinitive after 'disfrutar' (disfrutar hablar), but English requires the gerund: 'enjoy talking' NOT 'enjoy to talk'.

examples.en: Miranda enjoys talking to people when they have problems.
examples.es: Miranda disfruta hablar con la gente cuando tienen problemas.

examples.en: I'm really good with computers.
examples.es: Soy muy bueno con las computadoras.

commonErrors.wrong: Miranda enjoys to talk to people.
commonErrors.why: After 'enjoy', use the gerund (-ing form), not the infinitive.
Use 'good at' + gerund when describing an ability or skill.

grammar.title: Indefinite Article 'a/an' with Careers and Occupations
grammar.explanation: En inglés, usamos 'a' o 'an' antes de profesiones singulares. Decimos 'I'm a doctor', 'He's an engineer', 'She's a professor'. A diferencia del español, donde se puede decir 'Soy doctor' sin artículo, en inglés el artículo es obligatorio.
grammar.rule: Use 'a' or 'an' before singular occupations. Use 'a' before consonant sounds and 'an' before vowel sounds.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish speakers often omit the article: 'I'm doctor' instead of 'I'm a doctor'. Always include 'a' or 'an' before singular occupations in English.

examples.es: Ella es profesora de matemáticas en una universidad técnica.

commonErrors.correct: I'm a manager at a restaurant.
commonErrors.why: Always use 'a' or 'an' before singular occupations.

commonErrors.wrong: She wants to be a engineer.
commonErrors.correct: She wants to be an engineer.
commonErrors.why: Use 'an' before words starting with vowel sounds.

grammar.title: Prepositions with Fields of Study: 'in' and 'at'
grammar.explanation: Usamos 'in' para hablar de campos de estudio o carreras: 'a career in architecture', 'studying in medicine'. Usamos 'at' para instituciones: 'at a university', 'at City University'. En español se usa 'en' para ambos, pero en inglés la distinción es importante.
grammar.rule: Use 'in' for fields of study or careers; use 'at' for specific institutions or places.
grammar.spanishTrap: Spanish uses 'en' for both ('carrera en arquitectura', 'estudio en la universidad'), but English distinguishes: 'career IN architecture', 'study AT the university'.

examples.en: I'm studying for a career in architecture.

commonErrors.correct: I'm studying for a career in medicine.
commonErrors.why: Use 'in' with fields of study, not 'at'.
Use 'at' with institutions, not 'in'.

grammar.title: Yes/No questions with 'Do you' + verb
grammar.explanation: En inglés, para hacer preguntas con el presente simple, usamos 'Do you' + verbo en forma base. A diferencia del español donde solo cambiamos la entonación ('¿Trabajas en tu país?'), en inglés debemos usar el auxiliar 'do'.
grammar.rule: Use 'Do you' before the base form of the verb to ask yes/no questions in present simple.
grammar.spanishTrap: Los hispanohablantes a menudo olvidan el auxiliar 'do' y solo usan el verbo: 'You work in your country?' en lugar de 'Do you work in your country?'

examples.en: Do you work in your own country?
examples.es: ¿Trabajas en tu propio país?

examples.en: Do you use English in your work?
examples.es: ¿Usas inglés en tu trabajo?

examples.es: ¿Te gusta el inglés?

commonErrors.why: After 'do', use the base form of the verb, not -ing

grammar.title: Wh- questions with 'What' and 'Where'
grammar.explanation: Las preguntas con 'what' (qué) y 'where' (dónde) tienen estructura diferente al español. En inglés el orden es: palabra interrogativa + auxiliar + sujeto + verbo. En español podemos decir '¿Qué estudias?' pero en inglés debe ser 'What do you study?'
grammar.structure: Wh-word + do + you + base verb + complement?
grammar.rule: Use 'What' to ask about things and 'Where' to ask about places, followed by 'do you' and the base verb.
grammar.spanishTrap: Los colombianos a menudo olvidan el auxiliar 'do' en preguntas wh-: 'What you study?' en lugar de 'What do you study?'

grammar.title: Frequency adverbs: sometimes, often, all the time
grammar.explanation: Los adverbios de frecuencia indican qué tan seguido hacemos algo. En inglés van generalmente antes del verbo principal: 'I sometimes use English'. En español van en diferentes posiciones: 'A veces uso inglés' o 'Uso inglés a veces'.
grammar.structure: Subject + frequency adverb + verb OR verb + frequency adverb
grammar.rule: Frequency adverbs usually go before the main verb to show how often something happens.
grammar.spanishTrap: Los hispanohablantes tienden a poner el adverbio al inicio ('Sometimes I use English') que es posible pero menos común que ponerlo antes del verbo ('I sometimes use English').

grammar.title: Modal 'would like to' for wishes and preferences
grammar.explanation: Usamos 'would like to' + verbo base para expresar deseos de manera educada. Es más formal que 'want to'. En español decimos 'me gustaría' + infinitivo. La estructura es similar pero en inglés siempre necesitamos 'to' antes del verbo.
grammar.structure: Subject + would like to + base verb + complement
grammar.rule: Use 'would like to' followed by the base form of the verb to express wishes politely.
grammar.spanishTrap: Los colombianos a veces olvidan 'to' después de 'would like': 'I would like change' en lugar de 'I would like to change'.

grammar.title: Prepositions with places: at, in, with
grammar.explanation: Las preposiciones de lugar en inglés no siempre coinciden con el español. Usamos 'at' para lugares específicos como instituciones ('at a university'), 'in' para países o ciudades, y 'with' para personas. En español usamos 'en' para casi todo.
grammar.rule: Use 'at' for specific institutions, 'in' for countries, and 'with' for people.
grammar.spanishTrap: Los hispanohablantes usan 'in' para todo porque en español 'en' funciona para la mayoría de contextos: 'I study in a university' en lugar de 'I study at a university'.

grammar.title: Modal verb 'may' for possibility
grammar.explanation: En inglés, 'may' se usa para expresar posibilidad o probabilidad. A diferencia del español, donde usamos 'puede que' o el subjuntivo, en inglés 'may' va seguido del verbo en forma base (infinitivo sin 'to'). Es más formal que 'might'.
grammar.rule: Use 'may' to express possibility that something will happen or is true.
grammar.spanishTrap: Los colombianos tienden a traducir literalmente 'puede que' como 'can that', pero en inglés se usa 'may' + verbo base directamente, sin 'that'.

grammar.title: Present simple for habitual actions and general truths
grammar.explanation: El presente simple se usa para expresar acciones habituales, hechos generales y verdades universales. A diferencia del español, donde la frecuencia se marca con el contexto, en inglés a menudo se añaden adverbios como 'usually', 'often', 'always'.
grammar.rule: Use present simple to describe habits, routines, and facts that are generally true.
grammar.spanishTrap: En español decimos 'yo practico' igual que 'él practica', pero en inglés la tercera persona singular añade 's': 'I practice' pero 'he practices'.

grammar.title: Imperative for giving advice and instructions
grammar.explanation: El imperativo en inglés se usa para dar consejos, instrucciones o sugerencias. Se forma simplemente con el verbo base, sin sujeto. A diferencia del español, no tiene diferentes formas para 'tú' y 'usted'.
grammar.rule: Use the imperative form (base verb) to give advice, instructions, or suggestions.

grammar.title: Present Continuous for ongoing actions
grammar.explanation: El presente continuo se forma con el verbo 'to be' + verbo con -ing. Se usa para acciones que están ocurriendo en este momento o acciones habituales temporales. A diferencia del español donde se puede omitir el sujeto, en inglés siempre debe incluirse el pronombre o sustantivo sujeto.
grammar.rule: Use present continuous for actions happening now or temporary habits
grammar.spanishTrap: Los colombianos a menudo olvidan incluir el verbo 'to be' porque en español se puede decir 'yo estudiando' informalmente, pero en inglés debe ser 'I am studying'

grammar.title: Gerunds (-ing forms) as subjects and objects
grammar.explanation: Los gerundios son verbos terminados en -ing que funcionan como sustantivos. Se usan como sujeto de una oración o después de ciertos verbos. A diferencia del español donde se usa el infinitivo ('estudiar es importante'), en inglés se usa el gerundio como sujeto ('studying is important').
grammar.rule: Use gerund (-ing form) as the subject of a sentence or after certain verbs like 'helps', 'practice', 'enjoy'
grammar.spanishTrap: Los colombianos tienden a usar el infinitivo como sujeto ('to study is important') porque en español se dice 'estudiar es importante', pero en inglés es más natural usar el gerundio ('studying is important')

grammar.title: Modal verb 'can' for ability
grammar.explanation: El modal 'can' expresa habilidad o capacidad. Se usa con el infinitivo del verbo sin 'to'. En español se traduce como 'poder', pero a diferencia del español donde 'poder' cambia según el sujeto (puedo, puedes, puede), 'can' no cambia de forma.
grammar.structure: Subject + can + base verb / Subject + can't + base verb
grammar.rule: Use 'can' + base verb to express ability; it does not change form for different subjects
grammar.spanishTrap: Los colombianos a menudo agregan 'to' después de 'can' ('can to help') porque en español se usa 'poder' + infinitivo, pero en inglés es 'can' + verbo base sin 'to'

grammar.title: Sensory verbs: look + adjective
grammar.explanation: En inglés, usamos 'look' (parecer, verse) seguido de un adjetivo para describir la apariencia de algo. Es diferente del español porque en inglés NO usamos el artículo antes del adjetivo. Decimos 'looks delicious', no 'looks a delicious'.
grammar.rule: Use 'look' or 'looks' followed by an adjective (without 'a' or 'the') to describe how something appears.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian Spanish speakers often add an article before the adjective ('looks a delicious') because in Spanish we say 'se ve delicioso/deliciosa' with the article in the adjective ending. In English, no article is used.

examples.en: The meat looks delicious!
examples.es: ¡La carne se ve deliciosa!

examples.en: Which dish looks delicious to you?
examples.es: ¿Qué plato te parece delicioso?

commonErrors.why: Don't use an article before the adjective after 'looks'.
Use 'looks' (with 's') when the subject is singular (the food, the dish, the meat).

grammar.title: Expressing preferences with 'more my style'
grammar.explanation: Para expresar preferencias personales en inglés, usamos 'more my style' (más mi estilo). Esta expresión es común en conversaciones sobre comida y gustos. En español decimos 'más mi estilo' o 'va más conmigo'.
grammar.structure: Subject + is/are + more + possessive adjective + style
grammar.rule: Use 'more my/your/his/her style' to express personal preference or what suits someone better.
grammar.spanishTrap: In Spanish we might say 'es más de mi estilo' with 'de', but in English we don't use 'of' - we say 'more my style' directly.

examples.en: Actually, the sandwich is more my style.
examples.es: En realidad, el sándwich es más mi estilo.

examples.en: The meat is more your style.
examples.es: La carne es más tu estilo.

commonErrors.wrong: The sandwich is more of my style.

commonErrors.why: Don't use 'of' in this expression in English.

commonErrors.wrong: The healthy food are more my style.
commonErrors.correct: The healthy food is more my style.
commonErrors.why: 'Food' is uncountable in English, so use 'is', not 'are'.

grammar.title: Questions with 'What are you in the mood for?'
grammar.explanation: Para preguntar sobre deseos o antojos en inglés, usamos 'What are you in the mood for?' (¿Qué se te antoja? / ¿Qué te provoca?). Esta expresión siempre termina con 'for' en inglés, diferente del español donde no necesitamos una preposición al final.
grammar.structure: What + am/are/is + subject + in the mood for?
grammar.rule: Use 'in the mood for' to ask about someone's current desire or preference. The question always ends with 'for'.
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian Spanish speakers often forget the 'for' at the end because in Spanish we say '¿Qué se te antoja?' without a preposition at the end. In English, you must include 'for'.

grammar.title: I'd like to + base verb (expressing desires)
grammar.explanation: En inglés, usamos 'I'd like to' + verbo base para expresar lo que queremos hacer. Es una forma cortés de decir 'I want to' (quiero). A diferencia del español donde se usa 'me gustaría' + infinitivo, en inglés siempre sigue el verbo base sin 'to' entre 'like' y 'to'.
grammar.rule: Use 'I'd like to' followed by the base form of the verb to express what you want to do politely
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian Spanish speakers often forget the 'to' after 'like' or add an extra word, translating directly from 'me gustaría probar' as 'I'd like try' instead of 'I'd like to try'

grammar.title: Adjective + noun (regular/decaf, still/sparkling)
grammar.explanation: Los adjetivos en inglés siempre van ANTES del sustantivo, al contrario del español donde muchas veces van después. Por ejemplo, 'regular coffee' (café regular), no 'coffee regular'. Los adjetivos nunca cambian su forma en singular o plural.
grammar.rule: Place the adjective before the noun to describe it; the adjective form never changes
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian Spanish speakers may put the adjective after the noun, saying 'coffee regular' instead of 'regular coffee', following Spanish word order 'café regular'

examples.en: I'd like regular coffee.
examples.es: Me gustaría café regular.

examples.en: Bottled water is a beverage.

grammar.title: Food nouns with modifiers (nationality + food type)

En inglés, estos adjetivos SIEMPRE se escriben con mayúscula inicial, a diferencia del español. El orden es: nacionalidad + tipo de comida, por ejemplo 'Mexican tacos' (tacos mexicanos).
grammar.rule: Use the nationality adjective (always capitalized) before the food noun to describe food from a specific country
grammar.spanishTrap: Colombian Spanish speakers may forget to capitalize nationality adjectives (writing 'mexican' instead of 'Mexican') because Spanish doesn't capitalize them. They may also reverse the order following Spanish patterns.

examples.en: Mexican grilled fish tacos are delicious.

grammar.title: Future with 'I'll' for decisions made at the moment
grammar.explanation: En inglés, usamos 'I'll' (I will) para decisiones que tomamos en el momento de hablar, especialmente al ordenar comida. A diferencia del español, donde podemos usar presente ('tomo') o futuro ('tomaré'), en inglés es más natural usar 'I'll'. Es una contracción informal de 'I will'.
grammar.rule: Use 'I'll' when you decide something at the moment of speaking, especially when ordering food or making spontaneous decisions.
grammar.spanishTrap: Los colombianos tienden a traducir 'voy a tomar' directamente como 'I'm going to have', pero en restaurantes es más natural decir 'I'll have'.

examples.en: I think I'll start with the chicken soup.

commonErrors.why: Use 'I'll' for ordering decisions, not simple present

grammar.title: Polite questions with 'Would you like'
grammar.explanation: En inglés, 'Would you like' es una forma cortés de ofrecer algo o preguntar preferencias. Es más formal que 'Do you want'. En español, equivale a '¿Quisiera...?' o '¿Le gustaría...?'. Siempre va seguido por un sustantivo o verbo en infinitivo.
grammar.structure: Would you like + noun / to + verb
grammar.rule: Use 'Would you like' to politely ask about someone's preferences or to offer something.
grammar.spanishTrap: Los colombianos a veces usan 'You like' en lugar de 'Would you like', que suena muy directo y poco cortés.
